It identifies damping, relative stiffness, impact trajectory, bandwidth, and sensing delay as separate contributors and provides both less-conservative time-domain and robust-but-conservative input/output criteria.

assumptions: The user-supplied full text faithfully represents the accepted 1998 IEEE T-RA version despite extraction loss in many mathematical symbols.
The exact sufficient inequality is summarized structurally rather than reconstructed where OCR removed symbols; no stronger condition is inferred.
The operation index denotes repeated executions of the same prescribed task interval, and convergence is interpreted in that iteration index.

The paper's statement that exact dynamic knowledge is not required is interpreted as motivation for learning systematic feedforward action, not as proof of model-free operation under arbitrary uncertainty.
Experimental reductions in plotted errors are treated as author-reported evidence, not independent replication.
The term robustness is retained only as the authors' interpretation of convergence despite practical disturbances and varying contact points, not as a formal robust-stability guarantee.
boundary_conditions: The actual read source is the 1998 IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation journal version; only claims present in this file are included.
Learning is iteration-domain feedforward refinement over repetitions of a prescribed finite-duration operation, not continuous adaptation within a single novel task.
The target impedance and reference motion are supplied by the designer; the algorithm learns the feedforward input required to realize them, not the target mass, damping, or stiffness.
The manipulator operates in a finite workspace where the task-space Jacobian is nonsingular and joint-to-task mapping is one-to-one.
Robot inertia is symmetric positive definite, and the environment is modeled by a symmetric positive-definite linear stiffness relation.

The target inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices are positive definite, with additional symmetry conditions on matrix products used in the proof; diagonal choices are given as a sufficient practical case.
The theorem requires carefully chosen feedback, compensator, and learning gains satisfying a sufficient inequality involving norm and Lipschitz bounds; arbitrary gains are not covered.
Passivity or small-gain reasoning supplies boundedness of the within-trial interconnection; the iteration proof relies on local Lipschitz continuity and finite bounds of nonlinear robot terms.
The proof defines desired state, force, and feedforward signals that may be unknown and are used analytically rather than measured in implementation.
The environment stiffness and static position may be unknown, but the paper does not establish convergence for arbitrary time-varying, nonlinear, hysteretic, deformable, or active environments.
The same operation interval and prescribed action structure are repeated; generalization to dissimilar trajectories, durations, initial conditions, or tasks is not established.
Free-motion trajectory-error convergence follows as a special case when contact force is zero; during contact, nonzero position error can be the correct target-impedance response.

Higher gains proposed for lightly damped or stiff-contact cases may be limited in practice by actuator saturation, noise, sampling, and unmodeled dynamics, which are not incorporated in the stated theorem.

The experiment is limited to one three-degree-of-freedom SCARA, one path and contact-plane setup, one sampling configuration, and qualitative plotted convergence without reported confidence intervals or repeated-seed statistics.
Changing contact points observed in the experiment provide limited robustness evidence but do not constitute broad environment generalization.
The scheme avoids force derivatives and acceleration measurements but still uses force, position, and velocity information and a designed stabilizing controller.
claim: The actual read version is Cheah and Wang's 1998 IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation article, Learning Impedance Control for Robotic Manipulators. Here, learning means iterative learning over repeated finite-duration task executions: a feedforward control input is updated from trial to trial so that the closed-loop robot response converges to a prescribed target impedance, not neural-network training, reinforcement learning, or online discovery of the impedance parameters. A feedback controller and dynamic compensator maintain within-trial behavior, while the learned feedforward term reduces a reference-model or indirect impedance error across repetitions. Under the paper's gain inequalities, boundedness, smoothness, passivity, and task-space assumptions, the impedance error converges to zero; experiments on a three-degree-of-freedom SEIKO TT3000 SCARA report large error reduction across repeated free-contact-free operations despite unknown environment stiffness and contact location. The result advances fixed impedance toward repetitive-task refinement but remains tied to repeatability, a specified target impedance and reference trajectory, and restrictive convergence assumptions.
claim_locator: Actual read version: IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation, Vol. 14, No. 3, June 1998, pp. 452-465; Abstract and Section I; Section II, Eqs. 1-12; Section III, Eqs. 13-28 and Theorem with Remarks 3-6; Section IV, Figs. 1-11 and Eqs. 29-36; Section V Conclusion; Appendix proof, Eqs. 37-75.
content_summary: The paper reformulates iterative learning around a reference model rather than direct trajectory tracking. The repeated task has a reference trajectory, but successful learning is judged by whether the measured motion-force relationship matches the specified target impedance. This matters because unknown environment stiffness and contact position prevent prior derivation of separate desired force and motion trajectories. A within-trial feedback controller and strictly passive dynamic compensator provide stability, while a feedforward term is updated after each operation. The theorem gives sufficient convergence conditions through selected feedback and compensator gains and bounds on nonlinear robot terms; higher gains can satisfy the inequalities, and lightly damped targets or very stiff environments require higher controller gain because of larger overshoot. The method does not require force-derivative or acceleration measurement. In free motion, zero contact force makes convergence of impedance error also imply convergence of trajectory error. The same learning controller is retained across contact transitions. Hardware tests use a SEIKO TT3000 SCARA with one prismatic and two revolute joints, encoder-based position, differentiated velocity, an endpoint Lord force sensor, and a 244 Hz sampling rate. The repeated path includes free tracking, free-to-contact transition, compliant motion along a constraint plane, contact-to-free transition, and final free tracking. A steel ball reduces tangential friction. The first trial sets the learned input to zero and therefore provides feedback-only behavior. Across repeated operations, the reported impedance errors for all three joints decrease sharply, motion tracking errors decrease, and the contact-axis position error converges to a nonzero steady value consistent with impedance behavior under force rather than to zero. The authors also report convergence despite contact points changing across iterations, as reflected in the measured force. The paper does not learn the target mass, damping, or stiffness themselves; they are supplied as the desired model.
development_link: Classical impedance control required the programmer to specify both a target impedance and enough model knowledge for accurate realization. This work keeps the target impedance fixed but learns a repeatable feedforward control signal that compensates systematic robot and contact effects over successive executions, without requiring known environment stiffness or unloaded contact location. It unifies learning across free and contact phases without switching controllers. Relative to later adaptive and reinforcement-learning approaches, however, it does not select impedance online, generalize a policy across tasks, or explore uncertain contacts; its improvement is memorized along the repeated operation and depends on a prescribed reference, finite interval, stabilizing feedback structure, and convergence bounds.
epistemic_status: Full-text primary theory-and-experiment study of iterative learning impedance control. The convergence claim is theorem-supported only under the paper's stated system, gain, regularity, and repetition conditions; experimental trends are author-reported and were not independently reproduced. No conclusions are imported from other versions or from modern neural or reinforcement learning.

evidence.statement: The paper explicitly defines learning control as iterative generation of a control action for a prescribed repeated operation.
The learning objective is convergence to a target impedance or reference-model response, rather than direct convergence to separately specified desired motion and force trajectories.
evidence.support_scope: Section I and Section II, Remarks 1-2.

evidence.statement: Environment stiffness and the unloaded contact position are assumed unknown, so the desired force and motion trajectories cannot be derived in advance from the target impedance.
The target impedance uses positive-definite mass, damping, and stiffness matrices and is defined over a task space whose Jacobian is assumed nonsingular in a finite workspace.

The control structure combines stabilizing feedback, a strictly passive dynamic compensator, and an iteratively updated feedforward input; the impedance error enters the learning mechanism indirectly through a reference-model error.

The theorem states that, under the specified gain choices and sufficient inequality involving nonlinear bounds and Lipschitz constants, the target-impedance error converges to zero at every time in the operation interval as repetitions increase.
evidence.support_scope: Section III Theorem, Eq. 23-24, and Appendix Eqs. 37-75.

evidence.statement: The stability argument uses the interconnection of a passive robot system and strictly passive compensator, alternatively a small-gain argument, to ensure bounded motion and regularity needed by the iteration proof.
evidence.support_scope: Section III and Appendix around Eqs. 40-48.

evidence.statement: The paper reports that higher control gains can satisfy the sufficient convergence inequalities, and that lightly damped targets or very stiff environments require higher gains.
The learning law does not require measurement or estimation of contact-force derivative or robot acceleration.
The experiment uses a three-degree-of-freedom SEIKO TT3000 SCARA with encoder position, differentiated velocity, endpoint force sensing, and 244 Hz sampling.
The repeated experimental path includes free motion, entry into contact, compliant contact motion, exit from contact, and final free motion under one learning controller.
With the learned input initially zero, the first operation is feedback-only; reported impedance and trajectory errors then decrease over repeated operations.

The contact-axis trajectory error converges to a force-dependent steady value rather than zero, while the impedance error converges, consistent with learning a relation rather than pure position tracking.
evidence.support_scope: Section IV-B, Fig. 8 and surrounding discussion.

evidence.statement: The authors report convergence even though measured contact points changed between iterations.

evidence_kind: Nonlinear task-space formulation, passivity- and small-gain-supported iterative convergence theorem with sufficient gain inequalities, and author-reported repeated-operation hardware experiment on one industrial SCARA; no neural-network training, reinforcement learning, statistical multi-task evaluation, or learned impedance-parameter policy.
method_or_mechanism: The constrained manipulator is expressed in task space through a nonsingular Jacobian over a finite workspace. The environment is represented by a positive-definite linear stiffness relation with unknown stiffness matrix and unknown static contact position. A positive-definite target mass, damping, and stiffness define the desired impedance between reference acceleration, velocity, position error, and contact force. The controller combines a stabilizing feedback law, a strictly passive dynamic compensator with chosen gains, an intermediate state, and a feedforward learning input updated between operations by an iterative rule using an intermediate reference-model error. The impedance error does not appear directly in the update; the target relation is realized indirectly through compensator dynamics. The proof constructs desired but implementation-unknown state, force, and feedforward signals, uses passivity or small-gain arguments to establish bounded within-trial behavior and local Lipschitz properties, and defines an iteration-domain index function. A sufficient matrix and gain condition based on positive constants, norm bounds, and Lipschitz constants makes the index nonincreasing and forces the indirect model error, then the impedance error, to converge to zero for every time in the operation interval as the trial index tends to infinity.
problem_and_setting: Conventional iterative learning controllers refine prescribed motion or force trajectories, whereas impedance control specifies a dynamic relationship between reference-position error and interaction force and may not provide separately known desired motion and force trajectories. The environment stiffness and unloaded contact position are assumed unknown, making direct construction of the desired contact force and position histories unavailable. The paper asks how a robot performing the same finite-duration manipulation operation repeatedly can learn the feedforward action required to reproduce a given target impedance across free motion, entry into contact, compliant contact motion, exit from contact, and subsequent free motion.

inferred: The learned feedforward signal can overfit a repeated path and may not transfer to different trajectories, contact geometries, speeds, durations, or initial conditions.
Trial-to-trial changes beyond the theorem's bounded regularity assumptions can prevent monotonic refinement or convergence.
Increasing gains to meet conservative bounds may excite unmodeled dynamics, amplify differentiated-velocity noise, or exceed actuator limits.
Unknown linear stiffness is tolerated indirectly, but nonlinear, discontinuous, or changing contact mechanics may invalidate the fixed target and convergence analysis.
Because target impedance parameters remain designer-selected, the method does not solve optimal or context-dependent impedance selection.
The convergence result does not by itself certify safe behavior on early trials before the feedforward input has learned the repeated interaction.
reported: Conventional trajectory iterative learning cannot directly realize the desired impedance when environment stiffness and unloaded contact position are unknown and desired force and motion histories are therefore unavailable.
Separate learning controllers for free and contact motion require discontinuous switching at transitions.
Lightly damped desired impedance produces larger overshoot and requires higher feedback gain for the sufficient convergence condition.
A very stiff environment similarly requires higher controller gain.
The first feedback-only trial has substantially larger impedance error than later learned trials.
During contact, position error does not generally converge to zero because nonzero error is part of the desired force-motion impedance relation.

synthesis_role: Early variable-performance learning card showing the transition from fixed model-based impedance execution to trial-by-trial feedforward refinement of a prescribed impedance response. It establishes that the learned object can be the control input needed to realize a force-motion relation, rather than a force or position trajectory, and supplies a convergence proof and industrial-robot demonstration.

assumptions: The supplied full text faithfully represents the paper and equations.
The term accuracy means small error relative to the specified impedance relation, while robustness means attenuation of robot dynamics-model error and payload variation.
Author claims of a perfect solution are interpreted only within the ideal IMC algebra; the Evidence Card preserves the finite-delay and stability-condition qualifications.
Experimental values and comparisons are treated as author-reported and not independently reproduced.
The chosen Mbar_x and forgetting factors are assumed to remain within the theorem's certified region over the tested trajectory.
No inference is made that environmental stiffness uncertainty is comprehensively solved merely because the impedance relation uses measured force.
boundary_conditions: The desired impedance is a specified Cartesian linear mass-damper-stiffness model; the method improves realization but does not learn or optimize its parameters.
The ideal perfect-control statement assumes the IMC controller is the exact inverse of its internal model and the resulting closed loop is stable.
Exact cancellation of dynamics-estimation error occurs only in the zero-feedback-delay idealization; digital implementation has unavoidable delay and residual error.
TDE assumes the lumped unknown dynamics are continuous or piecewise continuous and change little over a sufficiently small delay, normally one sampling interval.

The controller still requires a kinematic Jacobian, a selected known inertia matrix Mbar_x, measured interaction force, and delayed acceleration and input force; it is model-light, not information-free.
The stability theorem establishes L-infinity boundedness, not asymptotic convergence of impedance error, passivity, or global contact stability.
The theorem assumes desired position, velocity, acceleration, and external force are bounded in L-infinity space.

Certified stability requires the induced-norm mismatch between actual Cartesian inertia and Mbar_x to satisfy Eq. 80 for all relevant time; arbitrary payload or configuration variation is not covered.
Forgetting factors must lie between zero and one; reducing them attenuates quantization history but weakens IMC robustness correction, while increasing them shrinks the certified inertia region.
Numerical differentiation makes velocity and especially acceleration sensitive to position resolution as sampling delay decreases.
A low-pass filter changes effective TDE behavior and is described as similar to lowering Mbar_x; filter phase and contact-energy consequences are not independently analyzed here.
The experimental target is deliberately overdamped with damping ratio 5; results do not establish equivalent behavior for lightly damped or time-varying impedance.
Experiments involve one planar 2-DOF robot, one stiff aluminum wall, one approach-slide-hold trajectory, one 1 kHz implementation, and one added payload.
DB-IC and IM-IC were excluded from later comparison because their free-space errors prevented task execution, so not every reported metric is a full all-controller comparison.
PB-IC and IM-IC inner-loop gains were tuned experimentally; conclusions depend partly on the chosen tuning and hardware.
The payload test demonstrates robustness to a 3.11 kg added load, not arbitrary mass, inertia distribution, or unmodeled flexible dynamics.
Force fluctuation near 3.7 Hz is dominated by motor-driver torque ripple, limiting inference about controller performance at that frequency.
The paper does not address unilateral transition criteria, multiple contacts, frictional stick-slip, deformable or active environments, actuator saturation, or safety bounds on peak force.
claim: The accuracy/robustness dilemma is the structural tradeoff that dynamics-based impedance control can reproduce a desired endpoint impedance accurately only when the robot model is accurate, whereas position-based impedance control attenuates model error through a high-gain inner position loop but allows the resulting inner-loop dynamics to contaminate the desired impedance and can even lose contact. The proposed method restructures the controller as an internal-model-control loop whose internal model is the desired impedance itself, then uses time-delay estimation to compensate unknown nonlinear robot dynamics from one-step-delayed input and acceleration. In the zero-feedback-delay idealization the IMC correction cancels dynamics-estimation error without inserting a competing impedance; with sampled delay, the residual impedance error is filtered by a factor proportional to 1-exp(-Ls), so accuracy is improved but not perfect. A conditional L-infinity stability theorem and 2-DOF SCARA experiments support bounded, more accurate and payload-robust behavior, but the method remains constrained by time-delay-estimation smoothness, sampling and sensor resolution, gain-region tradeoffs, acceleration estimation, and the tested single-contact setting.
claim_locator: Abstract and Section I; Section II-A-E, Eqs. 1-28 and Fig. 1; Section III-A-E, Eqs. 29-66 and Figs. 2-4; Section IV-A-D, Eqs. 67-73, Tables I-II and Figs. 5-12; Section V, Eqs. 74-77 and Fig. 13; Section VI; Appendix Stability Theorem, Eqs. 78-93.
content_summary: The paper first formalizes the dilemma using a nonlinear multi-axis robot. In dynamics-based impedance control, model error enters through the desired impedance dynamics directly, so exact target behavior is fragile. In position-based impedance control, adjustable inner-loop PD gains attenuate model error, but the inverse inner-loop dynamics remain in the error channel and corrupt the commanded impedance. Instantaneous-model impedance control retains this contamination. The proposed IMC structure adds a parallel model identical to the desired impedance, producing a correction term based only on dynamics-estimation error. With no feedback delay, the derived reference-position error is zero even when model error is present. With discrete delay L, the response error becomes the target-impedance inverse multiplied by (1-exp(-Ls)) and TDE error, which attenuates slowly varying error without adding a foreign inner-loop impedance. TDE avoids full dynamics parameters but needs Mbar_x, the Jacobian, recent input force, and numerically estimated acceleration. The practical recursive implementation eliminates the internal model state, adds forgetting factors to suppress cumulative quantization error, and may filter the TDE signal. The L-infinity theorem assumes bounded desired trajectory derivatives and external force and requires the induced-norm mismatch between Mbar_x and actual Cartesian inertia to be smaller than a bound determined by the forgetting-factor matrix. Larger forgetting factors strengthen IMC correction but shrink the admissible Mbar_x stability region, exposing a remaining stability-versus-robustness tradeoff. Experiments use a 2-DOF SCARA-type robot at 1 kHz against an aluminum plate of about 150000 N/m. The task approaches the wall along y, moves 0.15 m along x while maintaining contact, and then holds. The desired impedance is 20 kg, 900 N s/m, and 400 N/m per axis, with damping ratio 5. Without payload, the proposed controller has the smallest free-space deviation, impact force of 57.6 N versus 70.2 N for position-based control, smallest contact-force fluctuation, and smallest impedance error; position-based control reportedly loses wall contact six times. Dynamics-based and instantaneous-model controllers have excessive free-space deviation and are excluded from further task comparison. With a 3.11 kg endpoint payload, the proposed controller again has the smallest position deviation, force fluctuation, and impedance error. Against a disturbance-observer implementation, the additional IMC loop improves results; below the 3.7 Hz motor torque-ripple peak, force PSD is reported at about 30% of the DOB controller's, while high-frequency fluctuation is limited by hardware torque ripple.
development_link: Classic impedance control established a continuous force-motion target and later contact-stability work tuned damping against environment stiffness and delay. This work addresses a different bottleneck: reproducing the chosen impedance accurately when robot dynamics are uncertain. It progresses from full model cancellation or inner-position-loop robustness to a two-degree-of-freedom architecture that independently specifies command response and error correction, using recent data instead of full dynamics. It does not choose the impedance, adapt it to task context, or prove general contact-transition safety; later adaptive and learning methods still need to manage parameter selection, nonlinear and multi-contact environments, sampling-energy effects, and estimator uncertainty.
epistemic_status: Full-text primary controller-design and experimental-comparison study. Algebraic accuracy relations and the L-infinity stability condition are theorem- or derivation-supported under stated assumptions; experimental superiority is author-reported for the described SCARA task and was not independently reproduced.

evidence.statement: DB-IC attains the desired impedance accurately with precise dynamics compensation but directly transmits modeling error through the desired-impedance dynamics and lacks an independent correction gain.
evidence.support_scope: Section II-C and II-E, Eqs. 6-21 and Fig. 1(a).

evidence.statement: PB-IC attenuates model error with adjustable inner-loop gains, but model error excites inner-loop dynamics C^-1(s), which contaminate the desired impedance and can cause contact loss or oscillation.
evidence.support_scope: Section II-D and II-E, Eqs. 22-25 and Fig. 1(b).

evidence.statement: The proposed IMC uses the desired impedance as internal model and its inverse as IMC controller, adding a parallel correction term that depends only on dynamics-estimation error.
evidence.support_scope: Section III-A and III-C, Eqs. 29 and 33-40; Figs. 2-3.

evidence.statement: In the ideal no-delay IMC relation, desired impedance is realized exactly regardless of dynamics-estimation error, conditional on closed-loop stability.
evidence.support_scope: Section III-A and III-C, Eqs. 29 and 37-40.

evidence.statement: TDE estimates the unknown nonlinear dynamics from one-step-delayed Cartesian input force and acceleration, assuming the unknown term is continuous or piecewise continuous and L is sufficiently small.
With implementation delay, the impedance response error is proportional to the target dynamics inverse times (1-exp(-Ls)) and TDE error, so cancellation is effective but not exact for finite L.

The recursive controller removes real-time internal-model-state computation, but sensor quantization accumulates through IMC feedback; forgetting factors and low-pass filtering are introduced to attenuate it.
The stability theorem gives L-infinity stability for bounded desired trajectory, derivatives, and external force when the induced-norm inertia-mismatch condition in Eq. 80 is satisfied.
The admissible Mbar_x region depends on the forgetting factor; stronger IMC feedback can improve robustness but reduce the certified stability region.
Experiments use a 2-DOF SCARA-type robot at 1 kHz against an aluminum plate of about 150000 N/m, with desired impedance Md=diag(20,20) kg, Bd=diag(900,900) N s/m, and Kd=diag(400,400) N/m.
Without payload, the proposed controller reportedly produces a 57.6 N impact versus 70.2 N for PB-IC, the lowest fluctuation and impedance error, while PB-IC loses contact six times.
evidence.support_scope: Section IV-D, Figs. 6-9 and Table I.

evidence.statement: With a 3.11 kg endpoint payload, the proposed controller again reportedly has the smallest position deviation, force fluctuation, and impedance error.
evidence.support_scope: Section IV-D, Figs. 10-12 and Table II.

evidence.statement: Compared with impedance control using a DOB, the proposed controller adds IMC correction for uncompensated estimation error; below 3.7 Hz its contact-force PSD is reported at about 30% of DOB's.

evidence_kind: Nonlinear multi-DOF error-channel analysis, IMC and TDE controller derivation, finite-delay frequency-response comparison, conditional L-infinity boundedness theorem, and author-reported controlled comparisons on one 2-DOF SCARA with and without payload and against DB-IC, PB-IC, IM-IC, and DOB-based impedance control.
method_or_mechanism: The proposed architecture recognizes dynamics-based impedance control as an internal-model-control-compatible plant. A parallel IMC path uses the desired impedance inverse as controller and the desired impedance as internal model, so the difference between actual and model response feeds back an estimate-error correction. The IMC loop requires only desired mass, damping, and stiffness. Full robot dynamics compensation is replaced by time-delay estimation: Cartesian dynamics are partitioned into a chosen known inertia matrix Mbar_x times acceleration plus an unknown term H containing inertia mismatch, nonlinear dynamics, and interaction force. Assuming H is continuous or piecewise continuous and the delay L is sufficiently small, H(t) is approximated by the previous-step value Fu(t-L)-Mbar_x*x_ddot(t-L). The resulting torque command uses the Jacobian transpose, current desired impedance command, and one-step-delayed force and acceleration information. A recursive reformulation removes explicit real-time integration of the internal-model state. A diagonal forgetting-factor matrix attenuates accumulated quantization error in the recursive IMC feedback, while a first-order low-pass filter may be used in the TDE loop. The ideal no-delay algebra gives exact target impedance independent of dynamics-estimation error; the implementable delayed form leaves an error proportional to the delayed difference of TDE error.
problem_and_setting: Desired impedance is a Cartesian mass-damper-spring relation between trajectory error and interaction force. Direct dynamics-based implementation depends on estimated inertia, Coriolis, centrifugal, gravity, and friction terms and has no independent gain for suppressing model error; sensitivity is especially high for small desired stiffness and large desired mass. Position-based implementation improves robustness by commanding an inner position servo, but model error excites the inner-loop dynamics, which generally differ from the target impedance, degrading force-motion accuracy and potentially causing oscillation or contact loss. The paper seeks simultaneous accuracy, robustness to modeling error, and a simple implementation that avoids full online robot-model computation.

inferred: Rapidly varying discontinuous contact dynamics can violate the small-delay TDE approximation and increase residual impedance error.
Acceleration estimation and one-step delay can create noise-delay tradeoffs that become more severe with lower-resolution sensing or slower sampling.
The L-infinity theorem certifies boundedness rather than safe peak interaction force, so collision safety remains unresolved.
The stable inertia region may be difficult to guarantee across large workspaces, unknown payloads, flexible transmissions, or near-singular kinematics.
The architecture improves realization of a fixed impedance but does not solve context-dependent impedance selection or generalization across tasks.
Results from a planar single-wall experiment do not establish robustness for nonlinear, multi-axis frictional, deformable, active, or multi-contact environments.
reported: DB-IC is sensitive to dynamics modeling error, especially for small desired stiffness and large desired mass.
PB-IC improves robustness but its inner-loop dynamics distort the desired impedance and can produce oscillation or loss of contact.
IM-IC still suffers desired-impedance distortion from inner-loop dynamics.
Finite feedback delay prevents exact rejection of TDE error.
Recursive IMC feedback accumulates sensor quantization error unless forgetting or filtering is introduced.
DB-IC and IM-IC had excessive free-space position error in the experiment and could not execute the full task.
PB-IC lost contact with the wall six times and showed larger force fluctuation.
Increasing the DOB filter cutoff above 100 rad/s produced joint noise without further performance improvement.
Motor-driver torque ripple dominated remaining force fluctuation near 3.7 Hz.
Increasing the forgetting factor to enhance robustness reduces the certified stable range of Mbar_x.

synthesis_role: Robust-realization card in the development of impedance control. It separates the desired impedance from the error-correction dynamics, combines target-model IMC with model-light TDE, and shows that robustness need not be purchased by inserting an arbitrary high-gain inner position impedance. It also documents that sampled implementation replaces ideal cancellation with bounded residual error and a gain-dependent stability region.

assumptions: Interaction force is directly measured by a force/torque sensor.
The robot follows the rigid-manipulator dynamics and satisfies the stated unknown upper bounds on inertia, Coriolis/centrifugal, and gravity terms.
The virtual desired trajectory and its required derivatives are bounded; controller gains are selected so the Lyapunov terms are positive definite.
Repeated trials share a sufficiently repeatable finite time interval, target signal, and environment input-output relation for the betterment argument to apply.
The chosen cost/output map C(t), learning rates, initial impedance, and fixed apparent inertia are suitable for the task.
boundary_conditions: The environment class analyzed is linear time-varying mass–damping–spring dynamics in state-space form; nonlinear, hybrid, multi-contact, and unmodeled contact-transition cases are not covered by the convergence result.

Betterment convergence is finite-horizon and conditional on the contraction inequality, nonsingular C(t)B(t), and matching initial output; repeated-task invariance is implicit in applying one A(t), B(t), and target across iterations.
Desired inertia is fixed to apparent inertia because arbitrary inertia selection may destabilize the system; the paper learns only damping and stiffness.

Theorem 1 concerns the inner position-control loop and depends on bounded robot dynamics, bounded virtual-reference derivatives, positive-definite/tuned gains, and the specified discontinuous adaptive compensation; it is not a passivity or general stability proof for the full robot–environment learning loop.
The cost requires designer-selected scaling across position, velocity, and integral force quantities with different units; the paper acknowledges partial knowledge and trial-and-error may be needed.

Experimental evidence is limited to a wrist trajectory against one stationary human hand under time-scheduled contact/noncontact phases; no cross-task, cross-environment, or out-of-distribution transfer is tested.
claim: Li and Ge formulate impedance learning as repeated finite-horizon adjustment of a robot's time-varying desired damping and stiffness for interaction with an unknown, time-varying mass–damping–spring environment. Their outer loop uses gradient-following updates implemented through a betterment scheme, while desired inertia is fixed to the apparent inertia and a separate adaptive inner position loop tracks the virtual trajectory. The paper supports conditional convergence of the betterment process and theorem-backed inner-loop tracking, plus simulation and one human-hand interaction experiment showing iteration-wise cost reduction; it does not establish general coupled interaction stability, identify environment parameters, or demonstrate transfer beyond repeated versions of the studied task.
claim_locator: Section IV.B, equations (27)–(30), Theorem 1, and Remarks 5–6
content_summary: The paper combines two distinct forms of adaptation. The impedance-learning loop is an iterative optimization/betterment process over repeated interactions: it learns desired damping and stiffness schedules selected by a user-defined cost, not an environment model, desired trajectory, direct torque policy, demonstration mapping, or modern reinforcement-learning policy. The inner loop is continuous-time adaptive position control. Lemma 1 gives uniform finite-interval convergence for a generic linear time-varying betterment system under a contraction inequality, nonsingular input-output product, and matching initial output; Theorem 1 proves bounded closed-loop signals and asymptotic position tracking for the proposed inner controller under its robot-dynamics bounds and gain conditions. A six-DOF PUMA560 simulation uses an unknown synthetic time-varying diagonal environment, including a force discontinuity, and reports decreasing costs over ten iterations for tracking-dominant and compliance-dominant objectives. A Nancy robot wrist interacting with a stationary human hand likewise reports cost reduction and the expected stiffness/damping direction over iterations, with noisier learning than simulation.
development_link: Relative to early iterative impedance learning, the contribution is a direct betterment/gradient formulation for simultaneously adapting time-varying damping and stiffness without identifying the unknown environment, together with a regressor-free adaptive inner loop. The development remains trial-based and model-structured: the environment must fit the analyzed linear time-varying mass–damping–spring/state-space form, the task is repeated over a fixed interval, the objective and learning rates are manually selected, and desired inertia is not learned.
epistemic_status: qualified: mechanism and conditional analytical results are stated in the full text; performance findings are author-reported simulation/experiment, and generalization or coupled contact-stability claims are not established

evidence.finding: The unknown environment is parameterized by time-varying inertia M_E(t), damping C_E(t), and stiffness G_E(t); these quantities are declared unknown and used only for analysis.

M_d is fixed to the apparent inertia, while C_d(t) and G_d(t) are updated iteratively from tracking-error signals and the betterment output error; no environment-parameter identification is performed.
The generic betterment process converges uniformly on [0,t_f] only if the stated contraction inequality holds, C(t)B(t) is nonsingular, and the initial output matches the target.

For the specified adaptive inner controller and update law, with the paper's dynamics bounds and gain/positivity conditions, all inner-loop closed-loop signals are bounded and position error tends to zero.
evidence.locator: Section IV.B, Theorem 1 and Appendix B

evidence.finding: In PUMA560 simulations with a prescribed time-varying environment and a sudden removal of interaction after 1 s, the plotted cost decreases over ten iterations; changing cost weights shifts the learned impedance toward stiffer tracking or greater compliance.

For a Nancy wrist repeatedly interacting with a fixed human hand during 18 s trials, results at iterations 0, 5, and 10 show lower defined cost and impedance changes consistent with the selected tracking-versus-force weighting; the authors report noisy, less-smooth learning.

method_or_mechanism: The environment is represented for analysis as M_E(t)q̈+C_E(t)q̇+G_E(t)q=f with unknown M_E, C_E, and G_E. A target model maps force to a virtual reference q_r through desired M_d, C_d, and G_d. Because arbitrary M_d may cause instability, M_d is fixed to the apparent inertia; only time-varying C_d and G_d are iteratively updated. A cost/output error can weight position, velocity, and integral force tracking. Gradient-following updates for C_d and G_d are converted to a betterment law using measured position/velocity errors and the error between an environment output v and target v_d, avoiding explicit environment identification and explicit reinforcement-gradient estimation. Separately, a PD-like inner controller plus a sign-based adaptive term updates an unknown dynamics-bound estimate and tracks q_r without a robot regressor or learned dynamics model.
problem_and_setting: A rigid robot arm physically interacts with an environment whose time-varying inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices are unknown. The objective is not to estimate those environment parameters, but to improve a chosen interaction criterion through repeated trials while realizing a target impedance with an outer force/impedance loop and an inner position loop. Interaction force is assumed measurable by a force/torque sensor.

inferred: The paper does not prove passivity or stability of the complete outer impedance-learning plus environment interaction; the available theorem isolates inner-loop tracking.
Without projection or explicit positive-definite constraints in the reported update law, preservation of physically valid damping/stiffness matrices is not established by the presented text.
Because the betterment argument is trial-repetitive, substantial between-trial environment changes can invalidate its convergence assumptions even though within-trial parameters may vary with time.
The single scripted human-hand experiment and synthetic simulation do not establish generalization to novel tasks, contacts, or environment dynamics.
The sign-based adaptive term and direct force sensing may limit implementation where chattering, sensor noise, bandwidth, or force-sensor availability is problematic.
reported: Arbitrary choice of desired inertia may cause instability, so desired inertia is fixed rather than learned.
Learning rates are open parameters and are difficult to tune for sophisticated tasks.
A proper cost can require partial robot/environment knowledge and trial-and-error because it mixes differently scaled physical quantities.
Simulation shows overshoot when interaction is discontinued abruptly.
The hardware force signal is noisy and the experimental learning process is less smooth; the authors state these practical issues need further study.
The simulation discussion reports that excessively large PD gains or too small an adaptive matrix S may destroy stability.

synthesis_role: Marks a transition from fixed prescribed impedance and earlier task-specific iterative schemes toward structured variable-impedance learning in unknown dynamic environments: the learned object is an explicit time-varying impedance schedule, embedded in a two-loop controller with a separately proven adaptive tracking layer. It also exposes the enduring gap between cost improvement in repeated tasks and a general safety/stability theory for the full variable-impedance contact interaction.

assumptions: The manipulator obeys the accurately known rigid-body model and inverse dynamics cancels modeled inertia, Coriolis, gravity, and measured external torque as specified.
The reference and gain profiles exist beforehand and are differentiable enough to compute K̇ and Ḋ over the full task.
An α>0 can be found that satisfies both matrix inequalities for every time in the execution interval.
Gain matrices retain symmetry and positive definiteness.
For asymptotic stability, the semidefinite inequalities are strengthened to strict negative definiteness.
boundary_conditions: The theorem is sufficient, not necessary; stable profiles may fail the test, and the authors explicitly call it conservative.

The formal result is for unforced error dynamics τ_e=0. It establishes stability of the nominal variable-impedance system, not input-output passivity or stability with arbitrary active, uncertain, or nonlinear environments.
The desired inertia H must be constant, symmetric, and positive definite; stiffness and damping must be symmetric, positive definite, and continuously differentiable.

Implementation assumes accurate rigid-body dynamics, inverse-dynamics decoupling, and measurement of external effort. The authors state the method does not apply to simplified impedance control with configuration-dependent natural apparent inertia.
Cartesian implementation can violate the constant-H requirement near singular configurations.
Selection of α affects conservatism; a poor α can reject a profile that another valid α would certify.
The comparison with an energy tank is simulation-based and task-dependent; the authors make no general claim that either method is always less conservative.
The three 'real profile' cases are offline tests of data from prior studies, not new hardware trials demonstrating the proposed certificate under novel contact uncertainty.
claim: Kronander and Billard show that arbitrary time variation of impedance gains invalidates the standard fixed-gain energy argument: with constant virtual inertia, the classical storage derivative contains 0.5 q̃ᵀK̇q̃, so increasing stiffness can inject potential energy and produce instability even in free-space regulation. They derive a state-independent, offline-checkable sufficient condition coupling damping, stiffness, and both gain derivatives. Under exact dynamic decoupling and zero external torque, this condition guarantees global uniform stability, and strict inequalities give asymptotic stability. Simulations and offline checks of previously generated robot impedance profiles illustrate utility and conservatism, but the result is neither necessary nor a general passivity/contact-safety guarantee.
claim_locator: Section IV.B, validation of real impedance profiles
content_summary: The analysis pinpoints the energy source created by stiffness variation and extends the Lyapunov function with a position–velocity cross term so that admissible gain rates can be bounded without using the current robot state. Scalar special cases show that with constant damping, stiffness growth must satisfy k̇<2αk with d>αm; with constant damping ratio, a corresponding stiffness-rate bound is derived. The method is intended to screen impedance trajectories produced by geometry, optimization, learning from demonstration, reinforcement learning, or other generators, not to generate or learn them. Two one-degree-of-freedom simulations compare offline validation against a tank-based online limiter: one reproduces an unstable tracking profile and makes it valid by increasing baseline stiffness, while the other uses a validated regulation profile under temporary force perturbations and shows that the tank modifies stiffness particularly during perturbation. The authors additionally apply the matrix test offline to profiles from three prior works—a KUKA match-lighting experiment, a two-dimensional GMR/minimum-intervention reaching task, and a PI²-learned six-degree-of-freedom via-point task—and report that all pass the sufficient test.
development_link: Compared with classical constant-gain impedance, the paper makes explicit that time-varying stiffness is an active energy port and supplies a matrix condition that can be imposed on precomputed or learned profiles. Compared with online energy-tank stabilization, it trades state dependence and online profile distortion for advance certification and exact profile following, at the cost of exact dynamic decoupling, constant apparent inertia, direct external-effort measurement, and conservatism.
epistemic_status: qualified: the stability condition is theorem-supported and sufficient under explicit assumptions; comparative behavior is author-reported simulation and offline profile validation, not a general experimental proof of interaction passivity or robustness

evidence.finding: The classical energy derivative is −q̃̇ᵀDq̃̇+0.5q̃ᵀK̇q̃; a positive stiffness-rate contribution can inject energy whenever position error is nonzero.

For τ_e=0, constant symmetric positive-definite H, and symmetric positive-definite continuously differentiable K(t), D(t), existence of α>0 satisfying αH−D⪯0 and K̇+αḊ−2αK⪯0 for all time is sufficient for global uniform stability; strict inequalities yield asymptotic stability.
evidence.locator: Section III.A, Theorem 1 and Appendix B

evidence.finding: Scalar constant-damping and constant-damping-ratio cases convert the matrix theorem into explicit upper bounds on stiffness growth.

A one-degree-of-freedom sinusoidal tracking profile with mass 10 kg, damping 1 Ns/m, and baseline stiffness 12 is reported unstable; raising baseline stiffness to 18 makes it pass the proposed validation, while the tank method modifies the profile online.

In a validated regulation simulation with temporary constant-force perturbations, the proposed offline-certified controller follows the prescribed stiffness, whereas the tank-based comparator falls back toward constant stiffness when energy is unavailable.
The sufficient matrix test reports negative eigenvalues for three previously obtained impedance profiles: match lighting, GMR-based constrained reaching, and PI²-learned via-point motion.
evidence.status: author-reported offline validation of prior data

evidence_kind: offline validation of previously collected experimental/learning profiles
method_or_mechanism: For closed-loop error dynamics Hq̃̈+D(t)q̃̇+K(t)q̃=τ_e with constant symmetric positive-definite H and symmetric positive-definite differentiable D(t), K(t), the standard energy V1 gives V̇1=−q̃̇ᵀDq̃̇+0.5q̃ᵀK̇q̃ when τ_e=0. The authors introduce V2=0.5(q̃̇+αq̃)ᵀH(q̃̇+αq̃)+0.5q̃ᵀ[K+αD−α²H]q̃. Theorem 1 requires an α>0 such that αH−D(t) is negative semidefinite and K̇(t)+αḊ(t)−2αK(t) is negative semidefinite for every t. These are sufficient state-independent profile constraints; strict negative definiteness yields asymptotic stability. A practical eigenvalue-based check selects α from the minimum damping-to-inertia eigenvalue ratio and then validates or modifies the profile. Energy tanks are discussed and simulated only as an alternative comparator: they store dissipated energy and limit stiffness online when the tank lacks energy, whereas the proposed method validates a profile offline and then permits exact execution.
problem_and_setting: The paper addresses execution of an already specified time-varying stiffness and damping profile in an impedance-controlled rigid manipulator. Fixed-gain impedance is passive with passive environments, but arbitrary gain variation can destroy that property. The aim is to determine before execution whether a desired profile is stable, rather than to learn the profile or adapt gains online.

inferred: The theorem does not certify passivity of the time-varying controller at the external interaction port, so stable nominal regulation should not be read as a universal safe-contact guarantee.
Gain schedules learned online or altered unpredictably during execution cannot be certified offline unless their future values and derivatives remain within the theorem's inequalities.
Numerical differentiation and model/sensor error could compromise practical verification or implementation, but robustness margins for these errors are not analyzed.
The offline validation of prior datasets establishes feasibility of the test on selected profiles, not empirical superiority or generality across learned impedance tasks.
reported: Arbitrary impedance variations lose the fixed-gain passivity property and can produce unstable behavior even without contact.
The tank-based alternative is state dependent, cannot guarantee beforehand that the desired profile will be executed, and is sensitive to initial and threshold tank-energy levels.
The proposed certificate is conservative and may reject qualitatively stable impedance profiles.
A poorly chosen α can make the constraints overly conservative.
The constant-inertia requirement needs model knowledge, dynamic decoupling, and external-effort measurement, and is problematic in Cartesian space near singularities.
The method is inapplicable to the simplified controller considered by the authors when apparent inertia equals the configuration-dependent natural robot inertia.

synthesis_role: Provides a formal bridge between fixed impedance and learned or optimized variable impedance: learned gain schedules cannot inherit fixed-gain passivity automatically, so their rates and damping–stiffness relationship must be certified. It contributes an offline sufficient certificate for precomputed profiles while leaving profile acquisition, coupled contact passivity, model uncertainty, and less conservative certification unresolved.

assumptions: M(q) is symmetric positive definite, Ṁ−2C is skew-symmetric, and all modeled robot forces share a constant linear parameterization.
Desired position, velocity, and acceleration are bounded.
The damping weight remains bounded below by α1>0, and Kc, Γ, Λ and learning gains satisfy the positivity and Lyapunov inequalities used in Theorem 1.
One interval of sufficiently rich filtered regressor data occurs and can be stored accurately.
Interaction safety from passivity additionally relies on connection to a passive environment and compatible port/sign conventions.
Low-pass filtering and contact-torque sensing are accurate enough for the regression and mode weights.
boundary_conditions: The guarantee is specific to the proposed force-controlled CL-VIC law and its smooth weights; it does not cover arbitrary online, demonstrated, optimized, iterative, or reinforcement-learned impedance profiles.

Exact parameter convergence requires interval excitation: the filtered regression data must produce a positive-definite finite-window Gramian. Without that event, the proof only shows bounded estimator quantities, not exact identification.

The robot must satisfy the stated rigid Euler–Lagrange properties and exact linear-in-parameters structure with a known regressor and constant W; unknown nonlinear residual dynamics, changing payload parameters, and unmodeled actuator dynamics are not covered.

The exponential tracking statement applies when τe=0. During contact, the theorem's nominal result is boundedness/robustness and passivity of the τe-to-es mapping, not convergence to the desired trajectory.
Passivity is stated for contact torque τe and filtered tracking error es under the paper's sign convention; it is not a blanket passivity result for every physical port or for an active environment.

The proof's passivity step treats a model-error cross term as exponentially vanishing after interval excitation; the guarantee should therefore be read with the estimator-convergence and gain assumptions, not as independent of learning transients.
Contact torque, joint position, and joint velocity must be measurable or reliably available; filtering constants, thresholds, weights, gains, and excitation-window length are designer selected.

Experimental comparisons use one Panda platform and one constant-impedance composite-learning baseline; there is no direct comparison with offline-profile certification, tanks, RL, or other VIC algorithms.
The method is not validated on flexible-joint or underactuated robots; the authors identify that extension as future work.
claim: Pan et al. propose a force-controlled variable-impedance controller whose stiffness and damping are adjusted online by smooth functions of measured tracking error, filtered contact torque, and joint velocity, while a composite estimator identifies constant robot dynamic parameters from instantaneous and stored filtered torque-regression data. Under the paper's Euler–Lagrange model, known linear parameterization, interval excitation, gain conditions, and bounded references, Theorem 1 gives exponential convergence of parameter and tracking errors in free motion and passivity for the specified contact-torque-to-filtered-tracking-error closed-loop mapping. The method therefore avoids requiring a complete impedance profile to be fixed and certified beforehand, but it does not guarantee arbitrary learned gain schedules or interaction with arbitrary nonpassive environments.
claim_locator: Section II, equation (1), Properties 1–3, and Definitions 1–2
Section III.C, analysis of the three modes
content_summary: The learned quantity is the robot's constant dynamic parameter vector W, not an optimal impedance profile, environment model, trajectory, or reinforcement-learning policy. Variable impedance is generated directly online by prescribed smooth weighting functions. Theorem 1 states that under interval excitation, parameter error W̃ and tracking error e converge exponentially to zero when contact torque is zero; for bounded contact torque, the proof establishes bounded closed-loop signals. It also states passivity between contact torque τe and the filtered tracking error es under the paper's sign convention and gain conditions. This differs from offline certification of a known gain schedule: mode and gain changes respond to current interaction signals, and the stability analysis includes those weighting functions and the derivative of the weighted reference. Hardware experiments on a seven-DoF Franka Emika Panda compare CL-VIC with a composite-learning constant-impedance controller over five tasks: free-motion pickup, human guidance, polishing-like contact on soft and hard surfaces, and tripod-handle operation. The authors report comparable free-motion tracking, smooth mode transitions, lower contact effort with greater compliance, parameter-estimate convergence before interaction tasks, and a ten-subject human-guidance safety test.
development_link: Relative to Kronander-style offline validation, CL-VIC does not require the future stiffness/damping profile to exist in advance: impedance changes online through a designed multi-mode map, and its derivative enters the closed-loop reference dynamics. This is not a universal replacement for profile certification, because the guarantee applies only to this controller, weighting construction, estimator, and interval-excited linearly parameterized rigid-robot model. It also differs from impedance learning by demonstration, iterative optimization, or RL: composite learning here primarily estimates robot dynamics so the commanded impedance can be realized accurately.
epistemic_status: qualified: the estimator and closed-loop claims are theorem-supported only for the specified controller and assumptions; task performance and safety observations are author-reported experiments and do not establish guarantees for arbitrary learning strategies or environments

evidence.finding: The robot dynamics must admit a known linear regressor with an unknown constant parameter vector; interval excitation requires one finite window whose regressor Gramian is uniformly positive definite and is explicitly weaker than persistent excitation.

Smooth weights based on tracking/contact signals and velocity continuously vary the reference stiffness and damping across three modes, while regressor compensation uses the current parameter estimate.

Filtered torque/regressor data remove the need for acceleration measurement; the update combines instantaneous prediction error with an integral stored-data prediction error and freezes the informative window after interval excitation.
Under interval excitation and suitable gains, W̃ and e converge exponentially when τe=0; the proof also gives boundedness for bounded τe and states passivity from τe to es.

After parameter convergence, robot-dominant mode realizes precise constant-impedance-like tracking, collaboration mode varies impedance with contact/tracking signals, and human-dominant mode has zero stiffness while retaining damping.

Panda experiments across S1–S5 compare CL-VIC with CL-CIC and report similar free-motion tracking, increased compliant tracking error but reduced contact torque in contact tasks, and smooth transitions among modes.
Ten subjects performed the human-dominant interaction test; the paper reports an average peak contact-torque norm of 11.01 N·m and no apparent increase with peak joint velocity in the tested setup.

method_or_mechanism: Robot dynamics are assumed exactly linearly parameterizable by a known regressor Φ and an unknown constant vector W. Contact torque is low-pass filtered. A smooth stiffness weight ωs, driven by a weighted norm of filtered contact torque and tracking error, scales the reference velocity q̇r=(1−ωs)(q̇d+Λe): ωs=0 gives robot-dominant tracking stiffness, intermediate values give collaboration, and ωs=1 removes stiffness for human-dominant compliance. A damping weight ωd is bounded between positive limits and varies with filtered contact torque and joint velocity. The torque law combines ωdKc es with regressor compensation ΦrᵀŴ. Composite learning filters torque and regressor signals to avoid acceleration measurement, builds a finite-window data matrix Θ and integral vector ϕ, and updates Ŵ using both an instantaneous torque-prediction error and a stored generalized prediction error. Once interval excitation occurs, Θ and ϕ at the exciting time are retained, enabling exponential parameter convergence without persistent excitation.
problem_and_setting: The paper addresses physical human–robot–environment interaction with a rigid n-DoF robot whose numerical inertial, Coriolis, friction, and gravity parameters are unknown. It seeks online transitions among robot-dominant, collaboration, and human-dominant behavior while retaining accurate free-motion tracking, low contact effort, dynamic stability, and a passivity property without precomputing a full variable-impedance trajectory.

inferred: The claim of not depending on dynamic-model information means not requiring known numerical parameters; the controller still depends on a correct known regressor and linear parameterization.
A finite-window excitation condition may fail in slow, low-dimensional, or weakly excited tasks, leaving residual model error and weakening exact target-impedance realization.
Mode-transition thresholds and filtering can create task-dependent sensitivity or delay, but systematic robustness margins for noise, latency, and threshold choice are not established.
The experiments demonstrate selected task behavior rather than universal safety across collision severity, human behavior, or nonpassive environments.
Because the impedance map is hand-designed rather than learned for task optimality, the method addresses stable adaptive realization more directly than autonomous discovery of optimal impedance.
reported: Earlier variable-impedance methods based on experimentally determined stable regions require many trials and transfer only to similar environments.
Energy-tank approaches require task-specific energy bounds, which the paper identifies as impractical in some complex settings.
Force-controlled impedance can have poor free-motion tracking when model uncertainty prevents realization of the target impedance.
The proposed method requires interval excitation for exact parameter estimation, although this is weaker than persistent excitation.
The contact modes deliberately produce larger tracking error to keep contact torque small.
Flexible-joint underactuation is not handled and is left for future adaptation.

synthesis_role: Extends the development of variable impedance control from fixed or prelearned profiles requiring separate certification toward a jointly adaptive control-and-identification architecture whose restricted online gain-generation law is analyzed for stability and passivity. It narrows the model-uncertainty gap through finite-data composite learning, while retaining strong structural, excitation, sensing, and environment-passivity assumptions.

assumptions: The Cartesian robot obeys the stated rigid dynamics, M is positive definite, and Ṁ−2C is skew symmetric.
Model terms M, C, and gravity needed by the control law are accurately available, while contact force need not be measured for implementation.
SNEUM parameters satisfy the strict inequalities on directional weights and positive output weights, with positive quadratic and smoothing constants.
Dd(e,ė) remains positive definite for all relevant states.
The labeled set Ψ adequately covers the state region encountered during execution.
Continuous-time gradients and energy arguments remain representative after numerical evaluation, filtering, sampling, and robot actuation.
boundary_conditions: GAS is proved for the unforced nominal error system fe=0. With contact force, the theorem establishes passivity of the fe/ė port, not convergence, force bounds, or safety for arbitrary active environments.

The target Cartesian impedance must be realized exactly through the paper's structural choices Bd=M and desired damping C+Dd plus model-based feedforward of M, C, and gravity; robustness to compensation error is not part of the theorem.

The learned stiffness force must be a conservative gradient field of SNEUM and depends only on position error. Nonintegrable, history-dependent, contact-force-dependent, or broader policy representations are outside the proof.
Positive-definite state-dependent damping is required, but the paper calls its learning trivial and omits the detailed algorithm and certificate-preserving implementation.

Training requires labeled desired stiffness and damping samples. The paper lists demonstrations as one possible source but does not report learning the experimental laws from an actual human demonstration campaign.

Certificate constraints guarantee qualitative energy properties, not low approximation error to Ψ; feasibility and task performance still depend on data coverage, network size, hyperparameters, and constrained optimization.

For the accuracy-focused hyperparameter regime, theoretical stiffness can approach infinity near zero error; experiments use very large gains and low-pass filtering, without actuator-saturation or discrete-time stability analysis.

Experiments are limited to one Franka platform, position control with constant orientation impedance, one assembly setup, and one polishing setup; no transfer to unseen tasks or environments is demonstrated.
Baseline outcomes depend on authors' tuning, and the tank/optimization comparisons do not establish general dominance.
claim: Jin et al. learn state-dependent variable stiffness as the gradient of a constrained neural potential energy function, SNEUM, so stability is built into the learned force field rather than checked afterward from gain-rate bounds or maintained by online tank reshaping. For the exact Cartesian impedance error model, the paper proves passivity at the environment-force/velocity port during contact and global asymptotic stability of the unforced error equilibrium when damping and SNEUM satisfy explicit positivity, radial-unboundedness, unique-minimum, and parameter constraints. The guarantee applies to this conservative energy-gradient parameterization with model-compensated dynamics; it does not extend to arbitrary state-dependent policies, arbitrary contact environments, or uncertain realization of the target impedance.
claim_locator: Section V, equations (19)–(29), Lemma 1, and Propositions 1–2
Section VIII.B, robot polish experiment and Table I
content_summary: Theorem 1 establishes a general certificate: if Dd is positive semidefinite and the stiffness force equals the gradient of a positive-semidefinite differentiable V2, the nominal impedance system is passive with supply ėᵀfe; if Dd and V2 are positive definite and V2 is radially unbounded with a unique stationary minimum, the unforced equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable. Propositions 1–2 and Lemma 1 establish those properties for the constrained SNEUM, and Theorems 2–3 specialize the passivity/GAS results to coupled and decoupled learned controllers. A hyperparameter controls local behavior: values below one make stiffness grow without bound as error approaches zero to emphasize accuracy, while values above one make stiffness vanish near zero for smoother control. Experiments use a Franka arm. A nominally contact-free assembly task with 0.5 mm tolerance reports accurate completion and monotonically decreasing encoded energy. A contact-rich circular polishing task reports accurate periodic tracking; comparisons against a tank-based VIC, constant impedance, and an online-optimization VIC report smoother unreshaped stiffness and the best tabulated compliance, accuracy, and smoothness metrics under the authors' tuning.
development_link: Relative to offline rate certificates, SNEUM does not require K̇d or Ḋd and can be evaluated online as a function of state, but restricts stiffness to an error-dependent conservative gradient field. Relative to VICES-like policy learning, it does not jointly learn reference pose and six-axis impedance from task reward; it learns a stiffness-force map from labeled impedance samples while the motion planner/reference remains separate. Relative to composite-learning VIC, it learns the impedance law itself offline rather than identifying robot dynamics online and switching hand-designed modes; conversely, it assumes model-based compensation and provides no composite estimator for uncertain robot parameters.
epistemic_status: qualified: the energy-function properties and nominal impedance-system guarantees are theorem-supported; learning fit and task benefits are author-reported experiments, and robustness to model, sensing, sampling, or arbitrary-environment uncertainty is not established

evidence.finding: The storage V=0.5ėᵀMė+V2(e) yields passivity when Kd(e)e=∂V2/∂e and damping/potential are semipositive; strict positivity, radial unboundedness, and a unique stationary minimum give GAS for fe=0.

The SNEUM construction is shown, under its neural parameter inequalities, to be differentiable, positive definite, radially unbounded, symmetric in the sign of e, and uniquely minimized at the origin.
Constrained least-squares objectives fit the potential gradient to Kd,t et for coupled or axis-decoupled training data while enforcing SNEUM certificate constraints.

Coupled and decoupled SNEUM controllers inherit GAS for zero contact force and passivity at the contact-force/velocity port when damping is positive definite and the stated parameter constraints hold.
evidence.locator: Section VI, Theorem 2; Section VII, Theorem 3

evidence.finding: A Franka assembly experiment with 0.5 mm planar tolerance reports final x/y errors below tolerance, smooth control force, and total encoded energy decreasing monotonically to zero.
In circular polishing, the learned law tracks the periodic path; velocity noise produces noisy damping-related force, and low-pass filtering is applied before robot actuation.

The tank comparator sometimes replaces learned stiffness when tank energy is exhausted; after comparative tuning, the proposed method is reported best on the tabulated force, tracking, and smoothness metrics against tank, constant-impedance, and online-optimization baselines.
evidence.locator: Section VIII.B, Figure 6 and Table I

method_or_mechanism: The controller constrains desired inertia to the robot inertia and desired damping to C+Dd, yielding nominal error dynamics M ë+(C+Dd(e,ė))ė+Kd(e)e=fe and a force-sensor-free model-compensation law. Instead of fitting Kd directly, it enforces Kd(e)e=∂V2(e)/∂e, making stiffness-related force the gradient of a scalar potential. V2 is represented by a symmetric neural energy function, SNEUM: a constrained NEUM composed with an elementwise absolute-power transformation, plus a positive quadratic term. Positivity constraints on neural weights and directional parameters make SNEUM differentiable, positive definite, radially unbounded, symmetric in error sign, and uniquely minimized at e=0. Coupled and per-axis decoupled controllers are learned offline by constrained least squares that matches the SNEUM gradient to labeled stiffness forces Kd,t et; positive-definite damping is assumed or learned separately, with its learning details omitted.
problem_and_setting: The paper considers Cartesian compliant manipulation with stiffness Kd(e) dependent on position tracking error and damping Dd(e,ė) dependent on error and error velocity. A desired labeled set Ψ={et,ėt,Kd,t,Dd,t} is assumed available from a prior impedance law, human demonstrations, or expert specification. The objective is to learn a state-dependent impedance law that preserves task flexibility without an online stability filter reshaping it during execution.

inferred: Exact model compensation is a substantive hidden boundary: passivity/GAS of the target impedance does not by itself guarantee the implemented robot retains those properties under model error, delay, saturation, or filtering.
The integrable potential-gradient structure excludes some otherwise useful coupled stiffness fields and policies, trading expressiveness for certifiability.
Unbounded or extremely high near-origin stiffness may be physically unrealizable and can challenge sampled-data safety even when the continuous-time force field has a valid energy certificate.

Because experimental training labels appear prescribed rather than demonstrated or reward-optimized, the evidence supports stable imitation of a desired impedance map more strongly than autonomous discovery of task-optimal impedance.
Passivity supports stable interconnection only with a compatible passive environment; it is not a universal guarantee against impacts or active human/environment behavior.
reported: Tank-based reshaping is unpredictable, sensitive to tank settings, and can replace desired stiffness when tank energy is exhausted; the paper reports resulting force impacts in its polishing comparison.
Rate-certificate constraints are described as restrictive and primarily suited to time-dependent rather than state-dependent impedance.
The SNEUM hyperparameters used in the assembly experiment were selected by trial and error.
Learned stiffness and damping can reach values on the order of 10^5 because sampled errors are very small.
Velocity noise makes damping and damping-related force noisy, requiring low-pass filtering.
Residual polishing error is attributed to friction and uncompensated dynamics.
The conclusion acknowledges that stiffness depends only on position tracking error, limiting flexibility, and leaves contact-force adaptation for future work.

synthesis_role: Advances variable-impedance learning by replacing post hoc profile certification with a stability-certificate parameterization: the learned state-dependent stiffness force is integrable by construction as a neural potential gradient. It directly addresses state-dependent laws that cannot be cleanly assessed by time-derivative rate certificates, but leaves model-robust realization, contact-force-dependent stiffness, damping-learning rigor, and discrete-time implementation as open bottlenecks.

assumptions: The rigid manipulator admits the stated smooth forward kinematics and task-space Lagrangian representation over the operating region.
The desired reference xr is bounded and twice differentiable; the filter solution and required derivatives are bounded.
Desired impedance and feedback matrices have the positive-definite structure used in the derivation, commonly diagonal for simple filter integration.
Force/torque measurement error is bounded for the residual-set result and negligible for the stated asymptotic special case.
Task-space inertia, Coriolis/centripetal, and gravity terms and their derivatives satisfy the bounding relationships used in equations (14)–(17).
Adaptation and feedback gains are positive and chosen so the Lyapunov inequalities hold.
The relevant Jacobian/mapping remains physically realizable; redundancy resolution or augmented coordinates are selected consistently with the primary impedance task.
Continuous-time analysis adequately approximates the implemented sampled controller within the chosen gain and sampling regime.
boundary_conditions: This card covers only the 1991 IEEE CDC conference version actually read; conclusions or implementation details unique to the unread 1993 Journal of Robotic Systems extension are not transferred.
The desired impedance matrices M, B, and N are specified by the user and are not learned or adapted; the method adapts robot-control coefficients to realize that model.
The main result is global stability with convergence to a compact residual set under bounded disturbances and force/torque sensor error, not exact convergence in the general case.

The claim that the residual can be made arbitrarily small by increasing gains is derived in continuous time; the authors explicitly warn that discretization prohibits excessively large gains and mention moderate sampling near 100 Hz only through an external, unpublished simulation reference.
Asymptotic convergence is stated only when task-space dynamic terms are slowly varying relative to the adaptive elements and force/torque sensor measurement error is negligible.

The controller depends on Cartesian position, velocity-related quantities, desired-trajectory derivatives, measured contact force, and the task-space model structure/bounds used in the derivation even though numerical robot parameters are not required.
The paper does not formulate or prove passivity at the robot–environment port and does not analyze arbitrary active environments, impacts, switching contacts, delays, saturation, or multi-contact.
The F-to-T redundancy treatment is summarized at a high level and points to earlier mapping work; the conference paper does not provide a complete numerical implementation study.
No experiment or self-contained simulation result is presented, so practical robustness and computational claims are not independently supported within this source.
claim: In the actual read version—the six-page 1991 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control paper by R. Colbaugh, H. Seraji, and K. Glass, not the unread 1993 journal extension—the authors formulate direct adaptive impedance control as three linked components: a Cartesian impedance filter that converts reference motion and measured contact force into a desired end-effector trajectory, a direct adaptive Cartesian controller whose gains are updated without identifying the robot's physical parameters, and a Cartesian-force-to-joint-torque map that can exploit redundancy. Their Lyapunov analysis supports global boundedness and convergence of impedance-tracking errors to a compact residual set under bounded force-sensor error and modeled regularity bounds; the residual can be reduced by gains, while asymptotic tracking is stated only for slowly varying task-space dynamics with negligible force-measurement error. The conference paper provides no presented experiment and no general passivity guarantee.
claim_locator: Actual read version: Proceedings of the 30th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, Brighton, England, December 1991, pp. 2410–2415
Section 3, Adaptive Cartesian Impedance Control Scheme, equations (8)–(18)
content_summary: The paper contrasts indirect adaptive control, which estimates a linearly parameterized dynamic model, with direct adaptation of controller gains. Its architecture separates desired impedance specification from robot tracking and redundancy resolution. The filter requires only integration of a simple desired impedance model, especially simple for diagonal gains. The Cartesian controller is designed from a task-space robot model but assumes no detailed structure or parameter values beyond compatible dimensions and regularity bounds used in analysis. A Lyapunov candidate combines tracking errors with adaptive-gain errors.
