Across five additional free-space via-point segments, the controller reports centimeter-scale or smaller coordinate RMSEs; with robot torque limits artificially halved, the governor prevents reported saturation in every segment, while three segments saturate without it.

The authors explicitly state that their stability criterion is formulated for free-space dynamics, does not account for external contact, and currently excludes contact-rich and orientation-sensitive tasks.

method_or_mechanism: The reference motion is represented by a DMP whose forcing weights are optimized with episodic PI2. Instead of sampling damping D(t) and stiffness K(t) directly, C-GMS parameterizes matrix slacks SD(t), SK(t) with RBFs and enforces alpha H-D=-SD SD^T and Kdot+alpha Ddot-2 alpha K=-SK SK^T. It evolves a factor Q through Qdot=alpha Q+0.5 Q^{-T}B, B=-alpha Ddot-SK SK^T, and sets K=Q^TQ, making stiffness positive definite and the second inequality hold identically. Gaussian exploration therefore occurs in slack/trajectory parameter space while all reconstructed gain schedules remain inside this sufficient-certificate set. For torque feasibility, both slacks are uniformly scaled by sqrt(beta), beta in [0,1], which contracts gains affinely toward the baseline alpha H and preserves both inequalities; the largest beta compatible with per-joint torque boxes is selected analytically. PI2 then optimizes a task cost containing via-point tracking, acceleration, and stiffness penalties over certified rollouts.
problem_and_setting: The paper targets model-free learning of a Cartesian reference trajectory and time-varying impedance gains for compliant robot motion. Unconstrained PI2 exploration can lower task cost while sampling gain schedules that violate known variable-impedance stability conditions, and learned gains may also demand infeasible actuator torques. The concrete setting is a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 executing free-space, position-only via-point and handover motions under operational-space inverse dynamics; the formal nominal certificate sets external wrench to zero.

inferred: Calling every certified rollout 'safe' overstates the formal result: collision avoidance, interaction-force bounds, human safety, and environment-coupled stability are not certified.
The feasible manifold inherits the conservatism and model assumptions of the Kronander-Billard condition and may exclude useful stable gain schedules.
Uniform scalar gain contraction may be unnecessarily conservative when only particular directions/joints violate torque limits and may alter the learned compliance pattern.
The UUB result aggregates uncertainties into one bounded input and therefore does not identify robustness to structured model errors, delay, sampling, or estimator bias.
The limited free-space hardware tasks do not establish broad generalization, statistical reliability, or superiority over other certified learning architectures.
reported: Unconstrained sampling can reduce cost while violating the Lyapunov condition and producing oscillatory/divergent trajectories or gains.
The current certificate does not cover external contact, preventing direct application to contact-rich tasks.
The task objective and experiments omit orientation control.
Payload variation is not handled explicitly; extension of the governor to varying payloads is left for future work.

synthesis_role: Represents a post-learning development in which stability is no longer merely checked after a variable-impedance policy is learned: the policy search space itself is constructed from certified gain schedules. It is a useful bridge from offline stability screening to certificate-preserving exploration and actuator-aware execution, while also exposing the remaining gap between free-space internal stability and contact-port safety/passivity.

assumptions: Ensemble variance is a useful proxy for epistemic uncertainty and uncertainty-maximizing exploration yields adequate coverage of the task-relevant free-space state-action domain.
The learned one-step Cartesian model remains accurate enough under receding-horizon rollout for CEM to rank stiffness sequences.
A task can be expressed through fixed target state and quadratic tracking/stiffness costs without a separate high-level planner.
External force is sensed and included in the model input, and the low-level inverse-dynamics/VIC implementation realizes the intended Cartesian impedance sufficiently well.
The tied damping-stiffness rule is suitable across all tested tasks and ensures acceptable local behavior, despite no formal analysis.
Changing Q/R changes the objective without moving operation outside the domain covered by the generalized learned model.
boundary_conditions: The learned model is explicitly a free-space, unconstrained Cartesian impedance model; contact discontinuities and constraints are not represented.

The evaluation adapts translational stiffness only, keeps orientation stiffness fixed, uses fixed Cartesian goals, and couples damping to stiffness instead of learning full impedance matrices independently.
No Lyapunov stability, passivity, recursive feasibility, robust MPC, collision avoidance, or force/torque constraint guarantee is derived.
The physical model is not learned from scratch: a simulation-trained model is fine-tuned on hardware for 10,000 time steps, so claims of transfer should not be read as zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

Cross-task transfer is demonstrated on a small set of simplified objectives sharing one robot and related state/action structure; it does not establish transfer across robots, payloads, contact modes, or broad manipulation distributions.

Baseline policies are trained/retrained under different learning architectures and sample budgets; the paper reports normalized rewards and means but no inferential statistics or uncertainty intervals for the principal cross-method conclusions.
CEM planning runs at 5 Hz in physical experiments, while the low-level VIC runs faster; demanding contact dynamics may violate the time-scale separation assumed in the examples.
Cost weights Q and R directly determine the accuracy-compliance trade-off and require manual design/scaling for each task.
claim: Anand, Abu-Dakka, and Gravdahl propose deep Model Predictive Variable Impedance Control (MPVIC): a probabilistic ensemble neural model learns the Cartesian behavior of a robot under variable impedance using uncertainty-seeking exploration, and cross-entropy-method MPC repeatedly optimizes future stiffness values against task-tracking and compliance costs. The same learned free-space model is reused across several simplified manipulation objectives without task-specific model retraining, addressing a transferability weakness of learned impedance policies. Simulation and two Franka Panda experiments support qualitative stiffness adaptation and reported cross-task sample-efficiency advantages, but the method has no Lyapunov, passivity, or constraint guarantee; the authors explicitly identify discontinuous contact as potentially unstable and computation, contact-model omission, and manual cost weighting as important limits.
content_summary: The work positions deep MPVIC between task-specific RL impedance policies and analytical MPC. It first learns a generalized free-space Cartesian impedance model using random target/external-force excitation and CEM-based uncertainty maximization. The simulation model uses five three-layer, 256-neuron probabilistic networks and 100,000 samples at 10 Hz; for hardware it starts from the simulation model and fine-tunes for 10,000 time steps (reported as 33.33 minutes). The learned model is then reused for three MuJoCo tasks: compliant pose holding under sinusoidal force, catching falling objects, and pushing an object with friction. Two real tasks examine a tray under added objects and drawer opening. A SAC baseline and a PETS model-based baseline are trained per simulation task. The authors report broadly comparable normalized reward, with deep MPVIC better on the first task, similar on the second, and weaker on pushing, plus zero additional samples when reusing its model on tasks b/c versus retraining samples for the baselines. Behavior plots show stiffness rising when force/error or frictional resistance grows and falling when the objective permits compliance.
development_link: Compared with direct model-free RL/PI2 gain policies, deep MPVIC spends data on a probabilistic dynamics model and changes tasks through the online objective instead of retraining a policy. Compared with GP/PILCO-style model-based VIC, the probabilistic ensemble is intended to scale to higher-dimensional/nonlinear models while retaining uncertainty estimates. Compared with classical fixed/variable impedance control, the low-level mass-spring-damper relation remains, but stiffness scheduling is produced by finite-horizon learned-model optimization rather than a hand-designed adaptation law. The price is online CEM computation and loss of analytical stability/passivity guarantees.
epistemic_status: qualified: the reusable-model/MPC architecture and experimental settings are directly documented, while transfer and performance claims are author-reported comparisons on a small set of simplified tasks; no formal stability, passivity, safe-exploration, or contact-robustness result is provided

evidence.finding: The low-level Cartesian controller shapes a desired mass-spring-damper relation between external force and position/velocity/acceleration error; in evaluation, stiffness is the optimized action and damping is tied to stiffness rather than independently adapted.
A bootstrapped probabilistic ensemble captures output and ensemble uncertainty; CEM exploration maximizes ensemble predictive variance to collect data in uncertain free-space state-action regions.
At each step CEM-MPC optimizes a finite sequence of stiffness matrices on the learned model using task-error and stiffness-eigenvalue costs, executes the first stiffness, and replans.

The model uses five probabilistic networks with three 256-unit hidden layers; simulation learning uses 100,000 time steps, while the hardware model is simulation-pretrained and fine-tuned for 10,000 time steps before evaluation.

Across compliant holding, falling-object, and pushing tasks, plotted stiffness increases in response to large external force/error or friction and decreases when the target is approached; compliance weight changes the error-stiffness trade-off.

Normalized rewards are reported over 20 trials: deep MPVIC is better on task a, similar on task b, and SAC/PETS are better on task c; for transferring from task a to b/c, the reused MPVIC model requires no additional samples while SAC and PETS require reported retraining samples.
On a Panda, the controller increases stiffness as weights are added to a tray and initially raises stiffness to overcome drawer inertia before reducing it as the drawer nears its target.

The authors state that discontinuous-contact tasks are not supported and may become unstable because contact dynamics are absent; CEM computation limits control frequency, complex contact may require faster adaptation, and optimal cost weights are not obvious.

method_or_mechanism: A probabilistic ensemble of five neural networks predicts the next Cartesian state from current state, target, external force, and stiffness action while representing aleatoric uncertainty through probabilistic outputs and epistemic uncertainty through ensemble disagreement. During data acquisition, CEM-MPC chooses action sequences that maximize ensemble predictive variance, intended to reduce epistemic uncertainty broadly over the free-space state-action region. At deployment, another CEM-MPC samples stiffness sequences over a finite horizon, rolls them through the learned ensemble with trajectory sampling, and minimizes C=delta_s^T Q delta_s + lambda(K)^T R lambda(K), trading task-state error against stiffness magnitude/compliance. The first stiffness action is executed and the process repeats. Damping is not independently learned but tied to stiffness by the paper's critical-damping relation. Different tasks reuse the same model while changing/scaling Q and R.
problem_and_setting: Task-specific model-free and model-based variable-impedance policies often require retraining or fine-tuning when the manipulation objective changes. This paper asks whether one generalized Cartesian impedance dynamics model can support online stiffness adaptation for different compliant manipulation objectives simply by changing an MPC cost. The setting uses a Franka Emika Panda under low-level Cartesian VIC, with position-axis stiffness as the high-level action, tied damping, measured external force, and fixed goal positions.

inferred: Uncertainty-seeking exploration is not safety-constrained; high model uncertainty can coincide with unsafe robot states/actions.
Model exploitation can cause MPC to select gains that look favorable under ensemble predictions but perform poorly when all ensemble members share bias.
Absence of stability/passivity constraints means time-varying gains produced by MPC can violate known VIC energy/stability conditions even if short-horizon cost improves.
Tying damping to stiffness narrows the impedance behaviors available and may be inappropriate for anisotropic, coupled, or rapidly changing contact tasks.

The reported zero additional samples for task transfer reflects reuse of a previously trained/fine-tuned model plus new online MPC optimization, not zero computation or guaranteed out-of-distribution generalization.
reported: Non-continuous contact cannot be handled by the current model and may lead to unstable behavior.
Contact-aware state modeling is difficult and left for future work.
CEM has high computation time and trades optimization performance against control frequency.
The 5 Hz experimental adaptation may be insufficient for complex contact dynamics.
Optimal Q and R cost weights are not obvious.
The approach is not straightforward for complex manipulation and may require a separate high-level planner.

synthesis_role: Represents a model-predictive branch of learning-based variable impedance: rather than learning one direct impedance policy for one task, it learns a reusable robot Cartesian response model and performs online task-conditioned gain optimization. This separates reusable plant knowledge from task objectives, improving adaptation across a small demonstrated task family, while leaving certified stability and contact-aware modeling unresolved.

assumptions: Desired impedance parameters can be meaningfully estimated or updated online.
Required position, force, and/or EMG signals are available with sufficient quality for the selected method.
Controller and robot/human/environment models satisfy conditions required by any invoked Lyapunov, passivity, or optimal-control analysis.
Calibration and robustness procedures are adequate for task and user variability.
boundary_conditions: Physical HRI with online impedance/admittance adaptation.
Conclusions are survey-level and do not establish superiority of any individual method.
Stability claims are conditional on exact dynamics, sensing, controller design, and stated assumptions.
Performance and usability may vary by task, motion regime, user, and environment.
claim: Variable impedance/admittance control and learning strategies can support compliant human–robot physical interaction, but safe effectiveness depends on sensing quality, task and user conditions, controller assumptions, and explicit stability/passivity safeguards.
claim_locator: Controller-supplied full-text packet: definition and taxonomy of variable impedance control
Controller-supplied full-text packet: learning strategies and challenges
content_summary: The survey reviews roughly two decades of methods for varying or learning impedance/admittance during HRI. It distinguishes signal modalities and their trade-offs: velocity approaches can avoid force sensing but need task-specific calibration; force-based approaches regulate interaction force but require reliable force measurements; EMG-based approaches estimate intent or limb impedance but require wearable acquisition, processing, and robustness across subjects. It emphasizes that stability guarantees are architecture- and assumption-specific, and identifies safe adaptation, sensing reliability, generalization, and integration of learning with formal guarantees as unresolved challenges.
development_link: Supports development of an adaptive-HRI harness by motivating explicit representation of sensing modality, task/user calibration, controller architecture, and stability/passivity assumptions as first-class evaluation conditions rather than treating learned impedance adaptation as universally safe or superior.
epistemic_status: Author-reported survey synthesis; no independent verification or causal superiority claim inferred.

evidence.finding: Variable impedance control modulates desired inertia, damping, and stiffness online; velocity-, force-, and EMG-based approaches have distinct sensing and calibration trade-offs.
evidence.locator: Controller-supplied full-text packet: variable impedance definition and modality taxonomy

evidence.finding: Lyapunov, passivity/energy, and time-varying-gain constraints are discussed, but validity of a stability result depends on the modeled system, sensing, architecture, and assumptions.

Learning routes span adaptive/neural, optimal-control, GMM/GMR, DMP, reinforcement-learning, and demonstration/EMG-informed methods; open issues include safe adaptation, reliable sensing, and generalization.
evidence.locator: Controller-supplied full-text packet: learning and challenges sections

method_or_mechanism: A systematic taxonomy of impedance/admittance variation and learning methods: velocity-, force-, and EMG-based adaptation; neural/adaptive and optimal-control schemes; Gaussian mixture/regression and dynamic movement primitive representations; reinforcement learning; and demonstration- or EMG-informed approaches. Stability considerations include Lyapunov analysis, passivity/energy reasoning, and constraints on time-varying gains.
problem_and_setting: Physical human–robot interaction requiring online adjustment of desired inertia, damping, and stiffness to balance compliance/transparency, movement accuracy, and stability amid uncertain human and environmental dynamics.

inferred: A deployment that omits sensing-quality checks or stability/passivity constraints may adapt impedance unsafely under unmodeled human or environmental dynamics.
Treating this survey as experimental proof of a method's superiority would overstate its evidence.
reported: Velocity-based approaches can be task- and calibration-dependent.
Force-based approaches require reliable interaction-force information.
EMG-based approaches require wearable acquisition, signal processing, and subject-specific robustness.
Safe stable adaptation, generalization, and integration of learning with formal stability/passivity constraints remain challenges.

synthesis_role: Background and taxonomy source for framing design alternatives, sensing requirements, safety constraints, and unresolved research gaps in adaptive impedance control for HRI.
verification_status: Grounded only in the supplied controller packet; bibliographic and full-text claims not independently checked.

assumptions: The linear robot/force-sensor model contains the dominant instability-producing dynamics over the design band.
The impedance-magnitude cost over the selected log-spaced frequencies is a meaningful proxy for perceived or task-relevant low-impedance performance.
The bounded second-order environment set contains every human arm/environment the controller will encounter in its intended use.
Structured-singular-value calculations and the sampled frequency grid detect the relevant robust-stability boundary.
The implemented 1 kHz controller, sensing, and actuator reproduce the model closely enough that offline stability predictions remain informative.
The spring, block, and grasp tests are sufficiently exciting to expose unstable interaction for the tested conditions.
Measured friction and apparent inertia from slow force-position and initial-condition tests generalize to the relevant task amplitudes and velocities.
boundary_conditions: The analytical and experimental system is linearized and single-DOF with one dominant structural resonance and handle force-transducer dynamics.

Complementary stability guarantees coupling only with the explicitly modeled bounded environment set; an environment outside its mass, damping, stiffness, or structural assumptions may destabilize the nonpassive controller.

The human arm is represented as a second-order passive-like mechanical environment from prior literature; voluntary activation, reflex delay, multi-joint configuration changes, nonlinearity, and active devices are not comprehensively modeled.
The reported human-arm test is a vigorous grasp test without a stated cohort, protocol statistics, or adverse-event analysis; it is not clinical or population-level evidence.
The high-frequency lead controller identified in analysis was not implemented because force-sensor bandwidth was inadequate.
The robot model omits substantial Coulomb friction; the authors infer this may explain conservative stability predictions, but unmodeled dissipation cannot be assumed under all operating conditions.
Controller search is restricted to a chosen low-order pole-zero-gain family and frequency-domain cost; global optimality over controller structures is not established.
The natural-admittance comparison uses one platform and tested parameter sets rather than a general controlled benchmark.
No collision-force, tissue-load, fault, actuator-saturation, or multi-contact safety constraint is certified.
claim: Buerger and Hogan propose a computational loop-shaping procedure for interaction controllers that separates robot-port performance from coupled stability, searches controller pole/zero/gain space, and constrains the search either by passivity or by a less conservative complementary-stability condition. Complementary stability models the expected human-arm environment as a bounded set and converts stable coupling with every member of that set into a robust-stability test using the small-gain theorem and structured singular value. On one screw-driven single-DOF rehabilitation-robot module, the selected low-frequency lag force-feedback controller reduced Coulomb friction from 10-20 N to below 0.5 N and apparent inertia from 6 kg to 1.2 kg while passing the reported spring, hard-block, and human-arm tests more robustly than tested natural-admittance alternatives. The evidence supports the design idea and this actuator case, but not general multi-DOF human-robot safety: the environment set, linear robot model, controller family, single module, bandwidth limits, and non-statistical human testing sharply bound the conclusion.
claim_locator: Section V, Figures 14-15 and Tables I-II
content_summary: The paper first explains why interaction design differs structurally from ordinary servo design. It then applies computational loop shaping to a linear single-resonance model of a screw-driven robot with handle force-sensor dynamics. Under passivity, the search finds low-frequency lag/PI force compensation superior to proportional control for friction rejection. Complementary stability uses bounded human-arm inertia, damping, and stiffness from prior literature and identifies both lag and high-frequency lead regions with lower impedance cost than the passive design; the implemented high-frequency lead design was precluded by force-measurement bandwidth. A 1 kHz lag controller was tested against springs, a hard block, and vigorous human-arm grasp. Model predictions were conservative, possibly because unmodeled Coulomb friction dissipated energy. The controller was compared with natural admittance control and gave the better reported stability-performance combination on this platform. The conclusion identifies extension to multi-DOF/configuration-dependent systems as unresolved.
development_link: Compared with proportional force feedback and passive natural admittance, the method shapes feedback frequency response and searches the stability-performance surface. Compared with passivity, complementary stability is less conservative but only as trustworthy as the bounded environment model. Compared with later energy-tank or certificate-constrained variable impedance, it is an offline linear frequency-domain design for a fixed controller on a single-DOF actuator.
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical and robot-hardware evidence: the port-model design logic and bounded-environment robust-stability formulation are directly documented, and large impedance reductions are measured on one single-DOF module; no statistical human study, clinical outcome, multi-DOF validation, or universal interaction-safety certificate is provided

evidence.finding: Robot-port behavior determines interaction performance, while the robot-environment port-function product determines coupled stability; controller transfer functions do not enter these quantities as simple multiplicative loop-shaping factors.

A frequency-weighted impedance-error cost and passivity constraint are evaluated over pole-zero-gain grids; for the modeled module, low-frequency lag/PI compensation reduces impedance more effectively than proportional feedback while remaining passive.

Complementary stability requires robust stability for all environments in a bounded set; a second-order human-arm model with bounded mass, damping, and stiffness is tested using small-gain/structured-singular-value analysis.

Relaxing passivity to the bounded human-environment set lowers the best plotted normalized impedance cost from 0.72 to 0.50 and identifies nonpassive lag and lead controller regions predicted stable for the modeled set.

The selected lag controller ran at 1 kHz on one screw-driven single-DOF robot module; contact and impact tests used six springs, a hard plastic block, and vigorous human-arm grasp, while high-frequency lead compensation could not be implemented because of force-measurement bandwidth.
The implemented lag compensator reduced measured Coulomb friction from 10-20 N to below 0.5 N and apparent inertia from 6 kg to 1.2 kg, below the 3 kg passive limit stated for the model.

Within the tested spring, block, and arm conditions, the lag controller was more robust than the tested natural-admittance alternatives at comparable low-impedance performance; complete numeric table cells are poorly recovered from the supplied PDF text layer, so only the paper's stated comparison is retained.

The authors report a primitive optimization search and single-DOF application; extending the method to multi-DOF, configuration-dependent actuator or endpoint dynamics is nontrivial and left for further work.

method_or_mechanism: The method defines a frequency-domain cost from deviation between actual and target robot-port impedance and separately imposes a coupled-stability constraint. For a chosen controller structure, a computational grid searches pole, zero, and gain; at each pole-zero combination it finds the largest admissible gain and displays a design surface. First, positive-real port impedance enforces passivity. Then complementary stability replaces the all-passive-environments requirement with a set of expected environments represented by a nominal port function plus bounded uncertainty. For human arms, a second-order mass-spring-damper model with bounded real parameter deviations is used. The robot is inverted to admittance form and structured singular value/small-gain analysis tests robust stability across that environment set. This permits selected nonpassive controllers when their destabilizing environments lie outside the modeled set.
problem_and_setting: High-force human-interactive robots require low and tunable endpoint impedance together with high force capacity. Force feedback can suppress friction and inertia but threatens coupled stability. Classical servo loop-shaping tools do not transfer directly because robot-port performance depends on robot impedance alone, whereas stability depends on the robot-environment port-function product, and controller dynamics are embedded nonlinearly in robot impedance. The concrete platform is one screw-driven linear module intended for rehabilitation robotics.

inferred: If the environment uncertainty set is misspecified, complementary stability can authorize a nonpassive controller that is unstable with a plausible unmodeled person, tool, fixture, or contact geometry.
Coarse parameter/frequency grids can miss narrow instability regions or better controller structures.
Unmodeled Coulomb friction can mask instability during testing and may change with temperature, wear, lubrication, velocity, or load.
A pass/fail grasp test with an unspecified human sample cannot establish robustness across anthropometry, pathology, activation, or involuntary reflexes.
The large impedance reductions on one actuator do not directly imply safe or transparent behavior after integration into a multi-axis robot.
Robust coupled stability is not equivalent to task safety, comfort, clinical benefit, collision safety, or fault tolerance.
reported: Proportional endpoint force feedback that reduces apparent inertia too aggressively becomes nonpassive and vulnerable to contact instability.
Classical servo loop-shaping does not map transparently to interaction control because stability and performance depend on different port-function quantities.
The high-frequency lead controller could not be implemented on the hardware because of force-measurement bandwidth.
Natural admittance can drift in stiffness rendering because it feeds back velocity rather than position.
Nonpassive natural-admittance settings were less robust in the reported tests; settings matching lag-controller stability retained high inertia/damping and poorer performance.
The method had only been applied to single-DOF systems, and multi-DOF/configuration-dependent extension was unresolved.

synthesis_role: Represents an early explicit relaxation of universal passivity: controller design uses a bounded task/environment class to gain performance while retaining robust coupled stability for that class. It is a conceptual predecessor to environment-aware robust interaction design and constrained optimization of impedance policies.

assumptions: The momentum-based residual and dynamically consistent Jacobian inverse estimate external Cartesian force adequately despite neglected friction and Coriolis residuals.
The impedance controller realizes the desired decoupled mass-damper dynamics closely within the experimentally mapped region.
Reducing off-diagonal apparent-inertia terms is an appropriate proxy for matching desired task dynamics and improving stability.
End-effector speed is a useful proxy for human intent: low speed implies precision demand and high speed implies mobility demand.
The empirical stability region remains relevant along the drawn path and across the participants' arm impedance variations.
Path-length difference, execution time, and force norm adequately represent accuracy, speed, and effort for the selected writing task.
boundary_conditions: The main task controls only three-dimensional translation with zero desired stiffness; orientation and general six-dimensional impedance are not evaluated.
The dynamic-conditioning objective is local and task-selected; null-space motion can create collisions or rapid reconfiguration, and alternative orientation/task constraints may change the result.
Stability boundaries are based on vibration felt while an operator shakes one KUKA LWR4 near selected configurations, not a proof or instrumented universal criterion.
The applied null-space law is said to work in practice, but the paper acknowledges that a rigorous null-space stability proof would require a more complex controller.
The damping law and virtual masses are tuned for a single planar writing path and lightweight robot; the authors report worse behavior for an acceleration-based law on this platform.

Five participants perform the main comparisons and three compare the four impedance laws; participant demographics, repeated-trial counts, order randomization, effect sizes, and confidence intervals are not reported in the main text.
Participants are trained and blinded to controller identity but explicitly instructed to prioritize accuracy over speed, which can influence the time-error tradeoff.
The force-effort comparison and subjective comfort statements are descriptive and not cohort-level validated human-factors measures.
Statistical tests concern path-length error and execution time only; multiple comparisons and small-sample assumptions are not discussed.
claim: Ficuciello, Villani, and Siciliano combine velocity-dependent Cartesian damping with null-space redundancy resolution that locally minimizes dynamic coupling of a redundant robot's apparent end-effector inertia. On a 7-DOF KUKA LWR4 cooperative writing task, exploratory stability mapping and small within-subject comparisons indicate that inertia-decoupling redundancy supports lower virtual inertia than manipulability maximization, and that variable damping with low constant virtual mass offers a useful accuracy-time-effort compromise relative to high or low constant damping. Five participants support the main constant-versus-variable comparisons, with reported paired conclusions and p-values for execution time and path-length error, while only three test the four variable-mass laws and subjective comfort is reported informally. The study explicitly has no rigorous stability proof, uses hardware- and task-specific empirically felt vibration boundaries, and cannot establish general stability, causal superiority across robots/tasks, or comprehensive human safety.
claim_locator: Section VII-C-D, Figures 13-16 and Table I
content_summary: The paper derives the Cartesian impedance and force-estimation implementation, defines two redundancy objectives, and maps a stability region by having an operator shake the robot while damping and scaled virtual mass are varied until vibration is felt. In the selected configuration, damping 5-60 N s/m is reportedly usable when the mass scale exceeds 0.25, while below 0.1 vibration occurs for all tested damping. A scalar human-arm simulation motivates high damping at low speed and low damping at high speed, but acknowledges a constant 200 N/m human stiffness simplification. Hardware tests use a paint marker guided along a fixed planar path with straight lines, sharp corners, and arcs. With low inertia, dynamic-conditioning minimization completes the task while manipulability maximization tends toward instability. Five trained participants, blinded to controller identity and instructed to prioritize accuracy, compare redundancy and impedance options. Variable damping is faster than high constant damping (p=0.0062) with no detected length-error difference (p=0.9739), and more accurate than low constant damping (p=0.0094) with no detected time difference (p=0.8888). Force traces from one participant support lower effort than high damping. Three participants compare four mass laws, favoring low constant mass qualitatively.
development_link: The work extends Cartesian impedance control of redundant arms by using null-space motion to reduce mismatch between natural and desired dynamics, then schedules damping from observed velocity. Later passivity-filter work cites it as evidence that redundancy can enlarge the usable impedance-profile set, but replaces its empirical stability boundary with analytical sufficient conditions.
epistemic_status: qualified primary simulation, robot, and small human-participant evidence: the controller and experimental settings are directly reported, but stability regions are empirically elicited rather than proved, principal comparisons use five trained participants on one writing task, and some subjective and three-participant results lack formal statistical support

evidence.finding: A force-estimating Cartesian impedance controller imposes translational virtual inertia and damping; force feedback is required to reshape natural inertia.

Null-space control compares manipulability maximization with minimization of a weighted off-diagonal Cartesian-inertia cost intended to keep natural dynamics decoupled and closer to the commanded impedance.

Operator-induced shaking is used to mark vibration boundaries over damping and virtual-mass scaling; the resulting regions are robot-, configuration-, direction-, and procedure-specific, not analytical guarantees.

With a scalar constant-stiffness human model, velocity-dependent damping produces forces and velocities between low- and high-constant-damping cases; changing virtual mass adds little in this simulation.
At low virtual inertia, DCI minimization completes the writing task while manipulability-based redundancy tends toward instability; both complete it at a safer higher inertia.

Across constant and variable impedance conditions, DCI-based redundancy shows lower mean path-length error and execution time than manipulability optimization; all participants informally report better manual-guidance feeling with DCI.
Among four variable mass/time-constant laws, low constant mass L1 has the best plotted accuracy-time combination, but no inferential statistics are reported for this three-participant selection.

Variable damping is significantly faster than high constant damping (p=0.0062) without detected error difference, and significantly more accurate than low constant damping (p=0.0094) without detected time difference; the force-effort illustration is only one participant.
evidence.locator: Section VII-D, Figures 14-16 and Table I

evidence.finding: The authors state that no rigorous stability proof is provided, the modulation law is experimentally chosen, coupled human-robot theory is missing, and results cannot be generalized to arbitrary robots or tasks.

evidence_kind: t-test on path length and time
method_or_mechanism: A Cartesian impedance law uses external-force estimates derived from generalized momentum to impose a translational mass-damper relation with zero stiffness. A dynamically consistent generalized inverse isolates the end-effector task, while a projected null-space torque implements a secondary objective. Two objectives are compared: maximize kinematic manipulability, or minimize a dynamic-conditioning cost that heavily weights off-diagonal elements of Cartesian apparent inertia. The latter seeks locally decoupled end-effector inertia. Damping in each Cartesian direction is scheduled from high values at low speed toward a 5 N s/m floor at high speed. Four virtual-mass/time-constant laws are considered inside experimentally mapped stability regions; the selected L1 law holds virtual mass at 1.1 kg while varying damping.
problem_and_setting: In manual guidance, low damping and low apparent inertia improve mobility but can reduce accuracy or provoke instability, while high damping improves accuracy at the cost of effort and time. For redundant arms, internal configuration changes the natural Cartesian inertia and therefore how aggressively it can be reshaped. The paper asks whether redundancy can keep natural and desired inertia closer and whether online damping modulation based on operator motion can improve the comanipulation tradeoff.

inferred: Perceptual detection of vibration can vary by operator and may misclassify stability margins.
The apparent advantage of DCI can depend on the chosen planar path, initial posture, inertia weighting matrix, and absence of orientation control.
Small samples and incomplete reporting make p-values fragile and prevent reliable effect-size or population-level interpretation.
Velocity-dependent damping can switch too slowly or rapidly under noisy velocity estimates and may inject energy; no passivity analysis is provided.
Null-space motion optimized for inertia can violate collision, joint-limit, or ergonomic constraints unless those are added separately.
reported: With low virtual inertia and manipulability-based redundancy, the robot tends toward instability and the writing task cannot be completed.
For mass scaling below 0.1 in the tested stability procedure, vibration occurs for every damping value examined.
Low constant damping causes oscillatory force and velocity near stopping in the simplified simulation.
Acceleration-based damping adaptation performs worse on the lightweight KUKA because the system overreacts.
A rigorous theoretical justification for the modulation law and a stability proof for fixed and variable impedance are missing.
The experimental findings cannot be easily generalized to arbitrary robots and tasks.

synthesis_role: Provides task-level empirical evidence that null-space posture control and variable impedance should be designed jointly. It highlights configuration-dependent apparent inertia as a practical stability variable and offers a small human-guidance comparison, while serving as an example of useful but non-generalizable experimental tuning rather than certified VIC.

assumptions: The motor plant can be represented by the nominal LTI model times bounded multiplicative uncertainty over the frequencies of interest.
The identified uncertainty bound encloses end-use model deviations, including relevant backdriveability, friction, and load effects.
Robot and environment transfer functions are stable, square, and strictly proper when the mixed theorem is applied.
Environmental passivity holds in the low-frequency band and the robot-environment gain product is below one in the complementary band.
Frequency-domain gridding and the uncertainty-bound fitting procedure are sufficiently dense to represent the worst case.
Fixed-structure controller realization matches its continuous transfer function without destabilizing saturation or delay.
boundary_conditions: The main derivations use stable, square, strictly proper LTI single-port models; nonlinear high-DOF load dynamics are not covered by the presented guarantee.
Robust passivity covers unknown-phase multiplicative motor uncertainty only within the selected frequency-dependent magnitude bound.
Passivity relaxation also requires a model of the environment and a verified high-frequency gain-product bound; a stiff underdamped environment can make this difficult.
Passivity is a stability-oriented port property and does not itself bound impact injury, commanded motion, actuator torque, or human comfort.
Uncertainty is identified on one 1-DOF SEA setup under a small set of load and excitation conditions; intermediate loads are not directly verified.
The manually excited uncertainty estimate is noisier and excluded from the principal synthesis, while high-frequency uncertainty is extrapolated.
The observed low-damping violation demonstrates nonpassivity but finite experiments cannot validate passivity of the high-damping system.
Sampling and discretization are not part of the principal continuous/frequency-domain model.
claim: Haninger and Tomizuka extend impedance-control passivity analysis for flexible-joint robots with inner-loop torque control in two ways: robust passivity requires passivity for all multiplicative motor-model uncertainties inside a frequency-dependent magnitude bound, and a mixed passivity/small-gain condition permits high-frequency passivity violations when modeled robot and environment gains are sufficiently small. The results are conditional LTI frequency-domain guarantees, not universal safety proofs. In a one-degree-of-freedom series-elastic testbed, the authors identify uncertainty under no-load, fixed-output, and manual-excitation conditions, synthesize controller parameter bounds, and demonstrate energy extraction near 28 rad/s for a low-derivative-gain controller that satisfies nominal but not robust passivity. The experiment supports the value of uncertainty-aware design in this setup, while the paper explicitly limits generalization to identified load conditions, high-DOF robots, high-bandwidth discretization, and cases where a defensible uncertainty model cannot be obtained.
claim_locator: Section IV, Table I and Figures 5-6
content_summary: Analysis compares PD/PID torque control, nested velocity control, feedforward compensation, bandwidth-ratio heuristics, sensitivity, robust stability, and robust passivity. Higher motor or derivative damping improves robust-passivity margin; larger inertia, inner proportional gain, and rendered stiffness reduce it, while other parameters have frequency-dependent effects. A 1-DOF apparatus uses a Maxon motor, 1:132 gearbox, Bowden cables, and a 16.4 N m/rad torsional spring. Motor uncertainty is identified using motor-driven no-load and fixed-output sinusoidal tests plus manual load-side excitation. Using the first two uncertainty sets and an environment model, the authors choose a 60 rad/s passivity-relaxation frequency and derive parameter bounds. Two controllers share outer stiffness 8, outer damping 0.01, and inner proportional gain 15 but use derivative gains 0.1 and 1.5. Both meet nominal passivity; only the higher-damping case meets the identified robust condition. Manual excitation near 28 rad/s produces net energy extraction over a closed state trajectory in the low-damping case, confirming nonpassivity at the predicted frequency.
development_link: The paper connects interaction-control passivity to robust-control tools such as multiplicative uncertainty, the Cayley transform, sensitivity, and small gain. It complements earlier loop-shaping work by quantifying uncertainty margins and later gain-filter or MPC work by addressing fixed controller/model robustness rather than online time-varying impedance energy.
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical and benchtop experimental evidence: robust passivity and mixed passivity/small-gain results are conditional on stable strictly proper LTI models and bounded multiplicative uncertainty; hardware validation is one 1-DOF SEA system and demonstrates a passivity violation rather than validating universal passivity or human safety

evidence.finding: A load-side impedance and inner torque loop are modeled with flexible-joint stiffness and backdriveability; load dynamics and compensation error alter torque-tracking bandwidth and phase.
The Cayley transform yields a frequency-domain inequality that guarantees passivity for every multiplicative motor uncertainty below an identified magnitude bound.
For stable square strictly proper LTI robot and environment models, low-frequency strict passivity plus high-frequency small gain establishes input-output stability and permits finite-band passivity.

Derivative or physical damping generally increases robust-passivity margin, while larger inertia, proportional torque gain, and outer stiffness reduce it; robust passivity is more restrictive than robust internal stability.
evidence.locator: Section IV, Table I and Figures 5-6

evidence.finding: Frequency responses under no-load, fixed-output, and manual excitation are inverted to estimate motor-model deviations, with manual-excitation uncertainty larger at low frequency.

Identified uncertainty and a modeled load motivate a 60 rad/s relaxation frequency and bounds on fixed-structure controller gains; measured uncertainty is extrapolated above the tested range for robust-stability checking.
The low-derivative-gain controller, nominally passive but not robustly passive, yields net extracted energy over a closed trajectory during manual excitation near the predicted 28 rad/s violation.
Controller synthesis depends on defensible uncertainty identification and does not readily extend to integrated high-DOF manipulators; discretization may matter for higher-bandwidth systems.

method_or_mechanism: A flexible-joint load-side impedance architecture contains desired impedance I(s), torque controller C(s), motor dynamics G(s), physical joint stiffness K, environment E(s), and uncertain effective backdriveability. Nominal load-side passivity is expressed for the rendered torque/velocity transfer. Multiplicative uncertainty G=Ghat(1+Delta) with unknown phase and bounded magnitude is inserted, and the Cayley transform converts strict passivity into a small-gain inequality. A frequencywise search finds the largest uncertainty Delta_p that preserves passivity. Separately, the frequency domain is divided into a low-frequency set where robot and environment are strictly input passive and a high-frequency set where their gain product is below one, yielding coupled input-output stability under the stated mixed theorem. These tools are applied to fixed-structure inner torque and outer impedance gains.
problem_and_setting: Analytically passive impedance models can be nonpassive or unstable in practice because inner-loop torque dynamics, drivetrain backdriveability, friction, structural resonances, and model error are omitted. Classical passivity is binary and can also be excessively conservative at high frequencies where interactive robot and environment motion responses roll off. The paper seeks design metrics that expose robustness margin and rigorously relax passivity where a complementary gain condition can replace it.

inferred: Frequency gridding or extrapolation can miss a narrow resonance and overstate the robust-passivity margin.
An inaccurate environment model can invalidate the finite-band passivity relaxation even when the robot model is adequate.
The 1-DOF finding may not transfer to multi-axis coupling, configuration variation, nonlinear friction, or controller scheduling.
A design satisfying robust passivity can still deliver unsafe impact forces or undesirable commanded behavior.
reported: A robot with a passive nominal model can be unstable or nonpassive in a high-stiffness environment because passivity is limited by model accuracy.
Overcompensating backdriveability and velocity/friction feedforward can reduce passivity robustness by injecting or exposing energy.
Bandwidth ratio above ten has no rigorous implication for passivity and counterexamples can be constructed.
Manual excitation of the nominally passive low-damping controller extracts energy near 28 rad/s, demonstrating nonpassivity.
Extreme-load uncertainty may not generalize to intermediate loads, and uncertainty identification for high-DOF systems may be infeasible.
Without a motivated analytical or empirical uncertainty form, robust-passivity synthesis cannot be used.

synthesis_role: Provides an uncertainty-aware frequency-domain corrective to nominal passivity and a principled route to finite-band passivity. It is most informative for inner-loop design of flexible-joint interactive actuators and for understanding why nominal analytical passivity can fail on hardware.

assumptions: The robot dynamics and Libfranka model quantities are accurate enough for Cartesian feedback linearization and MPC prediction.
The time-varying mass, damping, and stiffness matrices satisfy the paper's positivity and storage-function conditions.
State, interaction force, and impedance parameters are measured or supplied with adequate bandwidth and low error.
The QP remains feasible and OSQP returns a usable solution within the 100 Hz top-loop period.
The chosen horizon and local linearization capture the energy effect of the complementary input.
Any upstream learned or hand-designed impedance profile is itself meaningful for the task; PMPIC only constrains its energy consequence.
boundary_conditions: The passivity port is f_in to r=e_dot+alpha e, not simply physical wrench to end-effector velocity; interpretation depends on this transformed supply rate.
The strict certificate uses z>=0. Choosing z_min<0 intentionally permits energy generation up to a selected bound and therefore relaxes strict passivity.
The controller assumes inverse-dynamics compensation and a locally linearized prediction model sufficiently accurate over the horizon.
The theorem does not include model uncertainty, sampling error, saturation, actuator limits, collision constraints, communication delay, or solver failure.
The cost penalizes only complementary input; task performance and safety depend on the externally supplied impedance schedule and other low-level limits.
The 26.92% result is one peak-input comparison against one filter under one simulation configuration, not a general conservativeness ranking.
The physical evidence is one brief sawing scenario on one Panda platform with no reported cohort-level statistics, comparator, injury metric, or force-safety threshold.
Passivity of the robot under assumptions does not establish safety against active humans, hazardous goals, excessive forces, or nonpassive environments.
claim: Cao, Cheng, and Li propose passive model-predictive impedance control (PMPIC), in which a lower-loop variable Cartesian impedance controller is augmented by a receding-horizon complementary force chosen to satisfy a dissipated-energy constraint while minimizing intervention. Their theorem establishes recursive feasibility and passivity for a transformed input-output port under the discrete prediction model and stated impedance conditions. Simulations show stabilization of a deliberately nonpassive stiffness schedule and a 26.92% lower maximum complementary input than one earlier passivity filter in a single configured comparison; a Franka Panda sawing demonstration with one operator shows the reported energy signal remaining positive. The analytical result relies on accurate inverse dynamics and prediction, the relaxed negative energy bound is not strict passivity, and neither the proof nor this one task establishes comprehensive physical-human safety.
content_summary: The controller runs a 1 kHz impedance loop and 100 Hz MPC using a locally linearized model and OSQP. In the first Gazebo/Panda simulation, a rapidly varying y-axis stiffness and very low damping cause an unconstrained variable impedance controller's dissipated energy and state trajectories to diverge; PMPIC activates a complementary force and retains the energy condition. A second simulation varies z_min and compares PMPIC with Bednarczyk et al.'s passivity filter. Strict z_min=0 intervenes more and produces smoother trajectories; negative bounds reduce intervention but allow bounded excess stored energy. Under matched settings, the paper reports PMPIC's peak complementary input as 26.92% lower. The physical demonstration is a 20-second push/pull sawing task on a Panda, with deliberate disturbances by the operator and another person, horizon 10, z_min=-0.01, and changing y stiffness. The plotted energy remains positive. Ethics approval and consent are reported, but participant count beyond the described operator is not given as a study cohort and no clinical or injury outcome is evaluated.
development_link: Compared with profile-shaping passivity filters, PMPIC leaves scheduled gains intact and modifies the apparent force input only when the predicted energy inequality requires it. Compared with energy tanks, it explicitly optimizes future intervention over a horizon. Compared with unconstrained learned impedance scheduling, it can accept learned gains as an upstream command but its certificate still depends on the analytical model and selected supply rate.
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical, simulation, and single-demonstration evidence: recursive feasibility and passivity are proved for the paper's modeled port and constraints, while lower conservativeness and safety claims are author-reported from two simulations and one Panda sawing demonstration with limited human-study detail

evidence.finding: Inverse dynamics is used to realize a time-varying Cartesian mass-damper-stiffness model, and passivity is formulated for input f_in and output r=e_dot+alpha e using a parameter-dependent storage function.
A dissipated-energy state is included in a discrete prediction model, and MPC minimizes complementary force subject to a nonnegative predicted energy constraint.

The paper proves recursive feasibility and passivity for the modeled system by constructing a feasible shifted control sequence and terminal input, assuming the stated model and strict energy constraint.
Allowing z_min<0 reduces intervention by permitting a bounded excess of robot stored energy over external supplied energy; this is an engineering relaxation, not strict passivity.

Under rapidly varying y stiffness and damping ratio 0.01, the unconstrained controller diverges after force application while PMPIC activates complementary input and keeps the reported energy condition.

With matched task and impedance settings, strict PMPIC is reported to require a 26.92% lower peak complementary input than the compared passivity filter; varying z_min illustrates the intervention-energy tradeoff.
A 20-second Panda sawing task with two staged stiffness behaviors and two deliberate disturbances retains a positive plotted dissipated-energy signal under PMPIC with horizon 10 and z_min=-0.01.
The authors identify accurate robot dynamics as PMPIC's main disadvantage and propose shorter horizons or robust MPC as partial or future remedies.

method_or_mechanism: Inverse dynamics converts the robot to a Cartesian double-integrator and a desired model Mv e_ddot + Dv(t)e_dot + Kv(t)e = f_in. PMPIC adds u_mpc to the right-hand side. Using r=e_dot+alpha e and a matrix storage function, the authors derive a dissipated-energy state z driven by the quadratic state dissipation and complementary input. A discretized linear time-varying prediction model augments robot error state with z. At each top-loop step, a quadratic program minimizes the finite-horizon sum of u_mpc^T R u_mpc subject to predicted dynamics and z(k)>=0; a configurable z_min<=0 relaxes that constraint. Only the first action is applied before replanning. The theorem supplies a feasible terminal input and concludes recursive feasibility and passivity under the strict zero lower bound.
problem_and_setting: Variable stiffness and damping can encode human demonstrations or task rules but may inject energy and destabilize physical interaction. Existing energy-tank or filter approaches can substantially alter the desired impedance. The paper asks whether MPC can compute the smallest complementary force that restores an energy inequality while preserving as much of a prescribed time-varying impedance profile as possible.

inferred: Unmodeled contact transients, torque saturation, or solver overruns can break the predicted energy balance despite nominal recursive feasibility.
A complementary force that is small in peak magnitude can still degrade transparency, comfort, or task intent, none of which is quantified in the human demonstration.
The transformed passivity output may obscure physical safety risks not captured by the selected storage function and supply rate.
A negative z_min requires an independently justified energy budget; choosing it ad hoc can turn a formal passivity claim into only bounded energy injection.
reported: A general variable impedance controller diverges in the deliberately low-damping simulation after the scheduled stiffness causes negative dissipated energy.
Stricter z_min near zero requires complementary force for longer and changes position, velocity, and acceleration more strongly.
More negative z_min reduces modification but can sacrifice safety when stored energy substantially exceeds supplied external energy.
MPC effectiveness relies on an accurate dynamic model; shorter horizons only partially relax this dependence.
Robustness to robot-model uncertainty is left for future work.

synthesis_role: Represents optimization-based passivity enforcement: rather than directly clipping stiffness or relying only on stored tank energy, PMPIC treats passivity as a horizon constraint and minimizes a complementary interaction input. It is a bridge between classical energy certificates and model-predictive variable impedance, with model dependence as the central tradeoff.

assumptions: Computed-torque control realizes the stated Cartesian impedance model closely enough for the derived storage inequalities to apply.
Desired and initial/final impedance matrices are symmetric positive definite and diagonal, with bounded positive damping.
Each switching variable remains in [0,1], is sufficiently differentiable where required, and follows the implemented min-based differential equation.
The filtered-error coefficient or matrix remains positive and bounded so bounded r implies bounded position and velocity error.
The selected filter rate beta and gain profiles are feasible at the implementation sample rate.
The environment is passive when passivity is used to infer coupled stability.
boundary_conditions: Virtual mass is constant; mass variation is outside the derivation.
Mass, damping, stiffness, and switching matrices are chosen diagonal so the analysis decouples by Cartesian coordinate.
The principal construction assumes stiffness increases and damping does not decrease; singular or opposing parameter changes require separate numerical handling.
Passivity is with respect to the filtered error r and external force under computed-torque linearization, not a direct guarantee of bounded contact force or human injury prevention.
The practical V4 filter uses a deliberately conservative replacement for a condition involving the second derivative of the switching variable.
The experimental result is one needle and one layered silicone phantom on one robot, with no human subjects, comparator trials, uncertainty analysis, or statistical outcomes.
The derivation is continuous-time; a 500 Hz implementation is reported without a sampled-data passivity proof.
Model error, torque saturation, friction-compensation error, sensor noise, delay, and coupled rotational adaptation are not part of the guarantee.
claim: Bednarczyk, Omran, and Bayle derive passivity filters for variable impedance control that either screen a prescribed diagonal stiffness/damping transition or reshape its scalar switching variables so derived storage-function inequalities remain satisfied. A first filter follows a known conservative condition; a second introduces a time-varying filtered-error matrix and a new storage function to admit faster, less conservative stiffness changes. Conditional passivity is analytical for the continuous, diagonal, constant-virtual-mass model and implemented profile constraints. A one-dimensional simulation supports reduced conservatism of the second condition, and a KUKA iiwa needle-insertion demonstration shows the filter limiting the rate of a stiffness increase while penetrating a layered silicone phantom. The paper does not test human interaction, broad task performance, uncertainty robustness, or comprehensive safety, and its practical filter is itself a conservative approximation to a derivative-dependent condition.
content_summary: The analysis begins with the standard variable mass-damper-spring error model and shows why the conventional kinetic-plus-stiffness storage cannot certify increasing stiffness. A filtered tracking-error storage gives two known matrix inequalities and a first scalar passivity filter. A generalized filtered error and Schur-complement argument lead to a second family of inequalities and a practical second filter. In a scalar simulation with mass 10 kg, stiffness 2 to 22 N/m, damping ratio 0.1, sinusoidal reference, and beta=10, the V4-based switching profile reaches its desired value faster than the V2-based profile while the corresponding storage derivative remains nonpositive. Hardware validation uses a KUKA iiwa 14 with an ATI Mini40 sensor and a 16G needle entering a four-layer silicone phantom. Translational stiffness is scheduled by material, virtual inertial terms are 5 kg, damping ratio is 1, beta=50, and control runs at 500 Hz. At skin puncture around 9.35 s, the filter constrains the change from 1000 to 3500 N/m.
development_link: The paper builds directly on Kronander and Billard's variable-impedance passivity inequalities, converting them into an explicit repair filter, and develops a less conservative storage function. Later PMPIC work compares against this filter and seeks to preserve the original stiffness profile by adding an optimized complementary force instead of changing gains.
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical, simulation, and hardware-demonstration evidence: passivity follows for the explicitly modeled diagonal impedance and filter inequalities; reduced conservatism is illustrated in one scalar simulation, and experimental support is a single robot-phantom needle task without statistical comparison

evidence.finding: For constant diagonal mass and time-varying diagonal damping/stiffness, a filtered-error storage function yields sufficient passivity inequalities; increasing stiffness is the relevant energy-injection case.
A scalar interpolation of each diagonal impedance term is rate-limited by the sufficient condition and combined with low-pass reference tracking to form the first passivity filter.
A time-dependent diagonal filtered-error matrix yields a new positive storage construction and sufficient inequalities involving the derivatives of damping and stiffness.
The exact condition contains gamma_ddot; the practical filter substitutes a more conservative rate bound h3 and takes the minimum of passivity and tracking limits.
The V4-based filter follows the desired switching profile faster than the V2-based filter in one configured mass-spring-damper example while its selected storage derivative stays nonpositive.
During layered-phantom needle insertion, the KUKA iiwa implementation at 500 Hz constrains the switching-variable rate when stiffness rises from 1000 to 3500 N/m at skin puncture.
The authors seek less conservative conditions and identify unusual transitions, such as increasing stiffness while decreasing damping, as requiring further investigation.

method_or_mechanism: After computed-torque linearization, the desired Cartesian error behavior uses constant diagonal virtual mass M and time-varying diagonal damping D(t) and stiffness K(t). Each parameter moves from an initial to final value through a diagonal switching matrix Gamma with scalar gamma_i in [0,1]. The first filter combines a low-pass tracking term beta(gamma_bar-gamma) with an upper bound on gamma_dot derived from the established storage function V2. To reduce conservatism, the paper replaces the constant filtered-error coefficient with a bounded time-dependent diagonal matrix B, derives storage V3, then sets B=D and defines V4. The resulting conditions involve D_dot, D_ddot, and K_dot. Because the direct bound would require differentiating a discontinuous min-switch output, a more conservative implementable rate limit h3 is substituted, yielding gamma_dot=min(h2,h3,beta(gamma_bar-gamma)).
problem_and_setting: Time-varying impedance can improve dexterity and adapt interaction to task or human state, but increasing stiffness may inject energy and destroy passivity. Existing conditions can determine offline whether a prescribed profile is passive but do not necessarily repair it, while energy tanks act online and depend on measured state and tank tuning. The paper seeks a profile-level filter usable offline or online that tracks a desired transition while enforcing passivity.

inferred: Rapid or coupled full-matrix impedance adaptations may not be representable by independent scalar switching variables.
Numerical differentiation, sensor noise, discretization, and rate saturation can violate the continuous inequalities at hardware level.
A filter can preserve passivity by slowing a clinically or task-critical stiffness change so much that task performance degrades.
The phantom demonstration shows implementability but cannot establish safety or effectiveness in real tissue or physical human-robot interaction.
reported: Arbitrary time variation, especially increasing stiffness, can destroy passivity of otherwise passive fixed impedance control.
The earlier V2 condition can be conservative and delay tracking of the desired switching profile.
The direct V4-derived filter is impractical because it requires differentiating a potentially discontinuous min-switch output.
The implementable filter therefore adopts a more conservative bound.
Increasing stiffness while decreasing damping can create singular or more restrictive cases and is left for further investigation.

synthesis_role: Provides a deterministic profile-shaping alternative to energy tanks and complementary-force MPC. It is useful when a desired gain transition is known in advance or generated online and can be restricted to the paper's diagonal interpolation form, but its guarantee does not cover arbitrary matrix-valued adaptation or implementation uncertainty.

assumptions: The robot satisfies the standard rigid-body skew-symmetry properties used by the storage-function proof and gravity is canceled sufficiently accurately.
The task field and, where needed, its potential or known Lyapunov function are available online.
Damping eigenvalues are nonnegative and the state-dependent basis remains well behaved away from the near-zero-field threshold.
The energy-tank coupling functions obey the stated inequalities and the initial tank state satisfies the stated positive upper-bound condition.
The contacted environment is passive when coupled-stability conclusions are invoked.
Selected gains and initial tank energy are adequate for friction, task duration, and expected disturbances.
boundary_conditions: The guarantee concerns passivity from external generalized force to robot velocity, not collision-force bounds, injury risk, workspace safety, actuator saturation, or task success.
The task field is assumed continuously evaluable with one stable equilibrium; discontinuities, multiple attractors, hybrid contact modes, and time-varying task fields are not analyzed.
Rigid-body structure and gravity cancellation are used in the proof; model error, delay, sampling, saturation, torque limits, and unmodeled flexible dynamics are not included.
For nonconservative fields, execution depends on a usable conservative/residual decomposition and finite tank energy; depletion suppresses residual task dynamics.
The damping basis is ill-defined when the desired field is very small and is handled by retaining the previous basis below a chosen threshold.
The controller cannot shape physical inertia in the presented formulation and does not provide a globally symmetric, independently specified stiffness around every point.
The empirical comparison uses one learned plate-in-rack task, three artificial target offsets, five runs per controller per offset, low gains, and no inferential statistics.
No human-subject experiment is reported, so claims about intuitive or safe human collaboration remain prospective.
claim: Kronander and Billard propose Passive Interaction Control with Dynamical Systems (PICDS), which closes the feedback loop around a state-dependent motion field, aligns a damping eigenvector with its desired velocity, and uses selective dissipation plus a finite virtual energy tank to render nonconservative motion fields while preserving passivity at the external-force/robot-velocity port. The analytical guarantee holds under the stated rigid-body, model-access, task-field, decomposition, and tank-coupling assumptions. In a robotic plate-in-rack task with deliberately misplaced attractors, five trials per controller in each of three perturbation settings show more consistent approach geometry, successful placement, and lower post-impact force than an open-loop-integrated trajectory tracked by low-gain impedance control. This is primary theory and a small task-specific robot experiment, not proof of general manipulation success or human safety; the paper explicitly says passivity is necessary but insufficient for safe human interaction and that tank depletion can degrade the commanded task behavior.
claim_locator: Section II, equation (1) and task assumptions
content_summary: The paper contrasts open-loop integration of a learned motion field with continuous state feedback into that field. It first derives state-varying selective damping, then a passive controller for gradient fields and an energy-tank extension for nonconservative fields. It explains decompositions available for LMDS, SEDS, and ELM-style stable fields and relates the controller to classical impedance: physical inertia cannot be reshaped without force sensing, orthogonal damping is explicit, and the drive field is stiffness-like only locally or where such behavior is encoded in the DS. A plate is inserted into a dish rack while the learned field's attractor is offset behind the real slot in three ways. For each offset, five runs use PICDS and five use an integrated reference with conventional impedance control. With deliberately low gains and no inverse dynamics, PICDS follows the curved approach more faithfully, places the plate consistently in the reported runs, and reduces post-impact contact force relative to the comparator.
development_link: The work extends passive velocity-field control by using directional dissipation and by making impedance tuning more explicit. It anticipates later passivity filters and model-predictive passivity constraints: all intervene on an otherwise performance-driven behavior to regulate net energy. Unlike gain-profile filters, PICDS acts directly on a state-dependent desired velocity field, and unlike later MPC methods it uses explicit coupling functions and a scalar tank rather than finite-horizon optimization.
epistemic_status: qualified primary analytical and experimental evidence: the passivity proofs are conditional on the paper's continuous rigid-body and energy-tank construction, while empirical advantages are author-reported from 30 controller executions in one plate-in-rack setup without inferential statistics or human participants

evidence.finding: The task field must be known and evaluable, continuous, and have a single stable equilibrium; the plant is represented by rigid-body dynamics, and passivity is defined at the external-force/velocity port.

A positive-semidefinite damping matrix whose first eigenvector follows the desired field selectively dissipates energy perpendicular to task motion and remains passive even when its orientation varies with state.
For a conservative task field, gravity cancellation plus velocity-error feedback is passive using kinetic energy and the field potential as storage.
For a conservative/residual decomposition, a bounded virtual storage state and specified gating functions preserve passivity while permitting stored dissipative energy to drive the residual field.

The controller cannot alter physical inertia; it exposes directional damping, and lambda1 f has a local stiffness interpretation near the attractor but need not define a symmetric stiffness around arbitrary points.

Three attractor-offset conditions are tested with five executions per controller; PICDS uses initial tank energy 10, lambda1=20, and lambda2=lambda3=200, while the comparison tracks an integrated reference with K=100I and no inertia shaping.

PICDS preserves the curved approach and reportedly places the plate correctly in all tested offsets; the comparator shortcuts the path, produces problematic final configurations, and has higher post-impact force.
The authors state that passivity is not sufficient for human safety and that finite tank energy can be depleted, forcing fallback to the conservative field and reducing task performance.

method_or_mechanism: For a continuous task field f(xi), the controller constructs D(xi)=Q Lambda Q^T with the first basis vector aligned with f and nonnegative damping eigenvalues. In a conservative field f=-grad(Vf), gravity compensation, damping, and the drive term lambda1 f yield a passive velocity-error controller with kinetic plus scaled potential storage. A general field is decomposed into conservative and residual components. A virtual energy state stores selected damping work and gates the residual drive so that nonconservative task power is released only from available stored energy; Theorem 1 establishes passivity from external generalized force to robot velocity for the specified coupling functions and initial bounded tank state. Conservative components can come from the original dynamics of a locally modulated DS or from the gradient of a known Lyapunov function. Perpendicular damping tunes directional compliance, while lambda1 f behaves locally like a nonlinear stiffness around the attractor.
problem_and_setting: Autonomous dynamical-system task models are commonly integrated open loop and then tracked by a position or impedance controller. That arrangement prevents the task field from responding directly to physical displacement of the robot and generally loses passivity when the reference velocity is nonzero. The paper seeks a controller that evaluates a stable time-independent task field at the measured robot state, moves along that field, dissipates perturbation energy orthogonal to it, and remains passive during uncertain contact.

inferred: A decomposition that is mathematically valid for passivity may still produce an undesirable conservative fallback path during contact.
The favorable plate-placement result may depend on the specific geometry and learned curved approach and may not generalize to other contacts or DS representations.
Force-estimation error visible before contact and absence of statistical testing limit quantitative comparison of contact force.
Sampling, torque saturation, and unmodeled dynamics could invalidate the continuous-time energy accounting in an implementation.
reported: Passivity is necessary but not sufficient for safe human interaction; an unsafe task field or aggressive velocity-feedback gains can still make PICDS dangerous.
Strong perturbations can sharply redirect a power-conserving controller; PICDS uses dissipation to avoid this but wastes energy.
A finite virtual store can be depleted, forcing fallback to the conservative component and degrading task performance.
The starting energy and tank upper bound are task-critical, especially if no meaningful conservative component can be extracted.
Both tested controllers track the nominal motion poorly because low gains and no inverse-dynamics compensation were intentionally used.

synthesis_role: Provides an early energy-tank and task-field branch of passive interaction control. It is especially relevant when a learned autonomous motion field should remain reactive to physical perturbations rather than being converted into a time-indexed reference, while illustrating that an energy certificate can coexist with substantial task-dependent performance and safety limitations.

assumptions: The normal contact can be represented by fe=Kenv(xe-xc), and the force-control direction can be analyzed independently from other Cartesian directions.
The position servo realizes the generated command and the measured force and its derivative are accurate enough for the PD/adaptive update.
Controller gains satisfy the stated sufficient Routh inequality for the actual impedance parameters.
The chosen initial adaptive compensation d(t0) is appropriate for the impending contact and does not itself create an unsafe command.
The desired force and environment signals meet the regularity and input-form assumptions used in the transfer-function and final-value arguments.
